From Bell's Weeklij Messenger, London > November, 10 1845. Foreign Intelligence. þÿ France. þÿ The French papers are occupied with two subjects ; the new scheme of Abdel Kader (tailing upon the inhabitants of Algeria to emigrate in a body to Morocco, and abandon the country without inhabitants to the French ; and secondly, what they call the progress of public discontent on account of famine in England. Nothing can be more atrocious than the heartless manner with which sorre of the papers treat this subject. ' It has pleased Providence," says one of the papers, " to enrich France with abundance, whilst England is in the midst of such general distress, as to render it necessary for her government to take into consideration the urgent necessity for suspending her cornlaws. Let us be duly prepared against this act of the English government. Our own aborning population must have bread and employment. We have, thank God, both one and the other this year, l.et us take care of them, and for that reason let us prevent the English from coming to satisfy their hunger at the expense of those gifts which God has reserved for 'is. This is a sad necessitv, no doubt, and at wh'c.h our humanity ought to lament. It would he more chivalrous to sacrifice ourselves for our neighbours, lutt good policy is not always consistent with chivalry. The French govei nnient ought to take care of the French population before it melts into pity for the sufferings with, which Ireland is menaced, England is, moreover, sufficiently rich, and has too many modes of

acting in the two hemispheres to he seriously embarrassed in supplying tbe deficiency of her crops. It is not for us, who have only as much as we want for ourselves, to supply her We repeal, therefore, if the measure in contemplation in England he carried into effect þÿ il England open her ports to the free importation of corn, our government ought to close ours. It is the right as il is the duty of that government."

Another French paper states, that the general distress in Belgium and Germany, and the apprehension of coming scarcity in England, for such doubtless are the causes, have begun to produce an alarming effect, on the French markets. " Provisions," says the journalist, " are every day becoming dearer in Paris. Folates are now double the price ihcv were a month since. The price of other vegetables rise in the same proportion. Poor families are already beginning to feel severely the effects of the had harvest. If this rise in the price of provisions increases in the same proportion for only one month, the necessaries of life will become beyond the reach of the indigent."

Another more serious statement is given in these foreign papers, namely that the Russian government is about to prohibit the exportation of corn f ront Odessa and the Euxine provinces, to any other hut a Baltic port, or to a Russian merchant for Russian use. It is also added, that the Turkish government is about to prohibit the importation of grain from any port in the Ottoman empire ; and that Naples and lite ports of Greece will be li'cned for the free importation of corn.

ST, $ 'Ji 0 2 IZ AT23. The Potato Crop in It eland. Latest Intelligence, London, Nov. 10. The intelligence received this morning is not of so favourable a character as that which arrived during last week. A change had taken place in the weather, which is now exercising a prejudicial influence upon the crop. Apple potatos, which, being of first qualitv, always fetch the highest prices, fell on Thursday in the Dublin market to 2s. 2d. per cwt., or Is. 4d. under the usual rates; the reason assigned for the fall being, that the apple having been the last crop planted, is considered to be tbe one that has suffered most by the contagion, and therefore the least fitted to be the subject of experimental trials towards preserving such portions as remain untainted. It is said, that fully twothirds of the stock of other kinds offered for sale in the Dublin markets on Thursday were bought up for the purpose of being manufactured into farina, in consequence of which, cups, tec., were sold at considerably advanced prices. In a letter from a remote district in Connaught the writer says. þÿ " Our potatos bete are nearly all infected with the disease þÿ some in the incipient stage, others further gone : and what we are to do with the people in such a district as this, except some extensive public work is undertaken to give employment, I cannot see. þÿ Much lasting injury has been done already bete by gratuitous relief in 1822 and (832, and no one who wishes this country weli could desire to see us again receivingclmrity." The Clare Journal contains tfie following

passage : þÿ " Without being guilty of the slightest exaggeration we may say that the situation of the potato crop is daily getting worse, and that consequently the prospects of the country are getting more alarming. We have already stated our opinion, that the case as we see it, and as thousands besides us see il, is so pressing, that not an hour should be lost in calling upon government to adopt such measures as wili keep in the country food sufficient to supply tbe wants of the people during the coming spring and summer. We see no way of doing so but stopping tbe exportation of corn, and prohibiting the distillation from grain." The Earl of Erne has called a county meeting in Fermanagh to consult upon the measures to be adopted in the present exigen cy, the potato crop having failed in that county to a great extent. measures of ti1e government. From the subjoined important announcement. which appeared in the Dublin Mail of Friday, it will lie seen that the executive government are taking further efficient means to provide against the contingencv of a scarcity in the staple food of the poor. " It is with unfeigned pleasure we announce þÿ which we do on authority þÿ that it is lite intention of government to appoint a commission of intelligent and experienced officers, to consider the measures which it may be proper to lake, with a view to provide against the expected scarcity of provisions from tbe failure of the potato crop. The selection of persons to form the commission has occa-

sioned some delay ; but the arrangements are now nearly completed, and we hope in a few days the commissioners will fie able to commence the arduous and responsible duties with which they will be intrusted. '

THE SANDWICH IS LA EDS. ( From a New York Taper.) The Petersburg, from Mexico, which arrived here on Friday, brings intelligence from the Sandwich Islands to the 20th ol May. Queen Pomare still remained at Keietea, blockaded by French forces, and on : of her chiefs, who aided in the assassination of some Frenchmen, had been shot by the French authorities. The Legislative Council of the Sandwich Islands, consisting of a House ol Nobles and a House of Representatives, convened on the 20th of May. The opening of the council was conducted with all the formality of the opening of the British parliament þÿ guns were fired from the forts, and the foreign vessels responded. The King's speech is in imitation of that of the kings of Europe. Peace is announced with all nations, and the attention of the legislature is directed to all matters of local or public concerns. The following paragraphs conclude the King's speech ; þÿ " We consider it the first of our duties to protect religion, and promote good morals and general education. It will therefore he your duty to consider by what means those blessings can be best promoted and extended among the people of these islands, and also among the foreigners resident in out dominions. We are well aware that the Word of God is the corner stone of our kingdom. þÿ Through its influence we have been introduced into the family of the independent nations of the earth It shall therefore be our constant endeavour to govern our subjects in tins fear of t he Lord; to temper justice with

mercy tn the punishment of crime ; and to reward industry and virtue. ' The Almighty Ruler of nations has dealt kindly with us in our troubles, in restoring our kingdom, together with special guarantees for its existence as an independent nation. May He also aid you in your deliberations, and may he grant his special protection to us, to you, and our people." When the King's speech was concluded, one of the Nobles, Governor Young, ofleted resolutions of thanks to the governments ol Great Britain, France, Belgium, and the United States, for recognising the iridependeuce of the islands, which passed unanimously. On the next day, the 21st, both houses replied to the King's address, concluding with " God preserve the King London Taper.

From Bell's Weekly Messenger< London, November, 10 1845. SOU I II AU-S T!l \TJ V. VV e have received South Australian jourua.s to the 17th of June. The colony was going on prosperously. The country is isceitnined to he rich m copper and iron, anil indications of coal have been lately met with. Wo subjoin an extract from one of the journals: þÿ " decent discoveries have abundantly confirmed the impression under which we penned the observations referred to, and we now with tireat pleasure and increased confidence invite the individual or collective co operation ot our fellow colonists in aid of our own endeavours to impress upon English capitalists the toll conviction of our vast, if not preeminei t local capabilities of production and adaptation lor the increasinglv indi-u disable branch of iron manufacture, conimoniv known as 'charcoal iron." Ever week's report of the mineral treasures of the pinvince contains a notice of some vast iron deposits, and every lour of exploration confirms our impressions of the incalculable sup. plies of wo .d fuel which may eas Iv he rendered available even in a country like ours, w hich has generally been described as not too thickly timbered for ordinary purposes." l'hc legislative council of Western Australia assembled on the 17th of April, when his Excellency Governor Hint opened the proceedings. Ilis Excellency regie's the difficulties and depreciations felt hv the farmers and stock holders, hut thinks former pi ices may have been too high, and is of opinion that capital may now, with existing ptices,

find profitable employment ; that the increase of stock is great ; that agricultural operations are extending; that the hill system and paper credits have given place to monev payments : that during the past financial vear imports have decreased, and the exports augmented 90 per cent., and the mercantile tonnage of the colony had attained to 800 tons. In reference to the vine and olive cultivation, his Excellency said that three vears only' had elapsed since the first steps were taken tor ties purpose. Each succeeding year had its vintage, and he knew no higher encomium which could he bestowed upon the wine of home growth, ot which some thousand gallons had this reason been made, than that during the last harvest it superseded, on some tarms, the use of ardent spirits. The cuituic ol the olive is following close upon that of the vine, and a latge quantity of olive oil lias been already prepared. The western Australians, who complain of the want of communication with the mother countrv, and the consequent lack of their remittances, talk of sending, periodically, the government schooner to meet the English mail steamers at Ceylon.

We copy the following inteicsting descrip tion of this island from the Friend of India: The island ot Chusan is seven miles from the mainland forty miles distant from the on v «l Niugpo. and lies in the vicinity of all the great and valuable marts of commerce on the eastern coast. It is 150 miles in circumference The chief hay, that of fmgliac,

JL 4 o :n o : i :z A T 2 3, is capable of accommodating, in perfect security, 100 sail of square rigged vessels, and possesses the most admirable facilities tor the establishment of docks Good water abounds, not only at the capital, but throughout the island. Chusan consists of a succession of hills and dales, which present one unbroken scene of rich cultivation, and exhibit the most lovely scenery. Wheat, rice, lea, grasscloth. sweet potatos. cotton, tobacco, and other articles grow in great luxuriance. The island is intersected wiih roads þÿ not intended tor wheeled conveyances þÿ from five to seven feet broad, and paved arid flagged throughout ; and it is thickly studded with villages. Ttiose who have the best opportunity of forming an opinion on the subject, believe that a hundred well populated towns and superior villages would be found on it, containing from one to five thousand inhabitants The w hole population is estimated at 270,900. The people are industrious and comfortable, and appear to have no want unsupplied ; scarcely a beggar is to lie seen, and ihere is a comparative absence of crime, whtch reflects no small credit on the Chinese character Not a single homicide lias occurred during the three years in which it has been in our occupation : and the inmates of the jail, conti ibiitcd by the whole island, have rarely exceeded 20; and of those the majority have consisted of those w ho wete confined for the illegal sale of its indigenous whisky, tfie stuunshoo. " The climate vies with that of the most

favoured regions in the world. It is the Alonipelher of China. There are but thiee monlits which can be called hot, June, July, and August. In this latter month the thermometer stands on an average at 80 deg ., but sinks at night to 70 deg. ; the next month it subsides to 71 deg , in the day. Then comes winter, with its bracing, o s. Iiili t ainig influences, and the gtound is covered with hoar frost, and the ice lies hall an inch thick . In Jnnuaiy and February the thermometer stands at 20. (leg of Fahrenheit. In March it rises to 28 iieg , but the hills continue to he capped with snow, and the cheerful fire is kept up nil the commencement of June, so that it is only during three mouths of the vear that woollen clothing is necessary. All the other places in China where we have commercial stations are hot, sultry, and unhealthy, and it is to Chitsan that invalids have generally resorted for the restoration of health and vigour. The island furnishes provisions nf eveiy description, of the best quality, at a very moderate price. Beef, pork, and poultry may he obtained in the greatest abundance. ()| geese, as largo iis those in England, there is no lack. Ducks are hatched by steam by thousands, and eggs are less than a halfpenny a piece. Game of every variety is easily procured. Bread, of English quality, is readily prepared by the Chinese. All kinds o! vegetables mav lie obtained, and English vegetables and fruits grow with great luxuriance. Potatoes have now been introduced, and will probably become an

article of great consumption throughout China. Indeed, all kinds of provisions triav be obtained at one-half the sum they cost at Hong Kong It is only for a European want to be known, to he immediately supplied fiom the island or the continent. Fish is obtained in the greatest abundance. Fishing is universal around the island, and it is calculated that not fewer than 70.000 vessels come from the continent, and remain for three months oil
Chusan employed in fishing. They are attended by boats filled with ice, in which the fish are packed, and then despatched lo lire neighbouring coast." þÿ Ibid.

It is a description of the character of Thomas f dwcelt the murderer, now in St. Thomas' fort. As the circumstances relating to the conviction ol this ill disposed man are known in this Island as well as in M. Thomas, we suspect that the following will not he uninteresting to our readers : Prisoner hi lions in the Fort, (St. Thomas.) "This seems a large head, the basilar, and occipital regions are above the usual size ; .so, also, are the lateral parts of the brain. þÿ The frontal configuration does not present an intellectual aspect. " 1 do not consider this a man of courage þÿ one who will fearlessly meet danger and strive to overcome it. He is cunning and deceitf ul ; he will lay his plans for carrying his designs into execution, hut he will not openly prosecute them if he think that there will be any strong opposition. He will rather wait for a favorable opportunity; which, when it arrives, he is not likely to allow to pass unavailed of. He has the cerebral conformation ol a cruel inhuman being ; Destructiveness, tirmness, Self- Esteem, Secretive ness, and Acquisitiveness, ate all very large. There is but little strength of the higher moral feelings, Conscientiousness, Benevolence & Veneration are but feebly developed, compared with those previously mentioned. " lie has great firmness, even obstinacy of

purpose; one.e a project is formed it will never be given up hut wiili life, no matter how long circumstances mav compel him to delay its execution. His plans will show more cunning than caution. He is perhaps rash in some instances, owing to a want ol circumspection in calculating their probable results. He is not capable of forming close friendships þÿ he is loo selfish and too jealous ; from this cause he is likely to he alone in all that he does þÿ his suspicious naiute makes him fear betrayal should he have an accomplice. " lie has great confidence in his own powers and resources, and feels much sell-importance. An insult will never he pardoned. He is likely to treat his etpials ami those below him, (il any), with haughtiness and severity. Discovery of the Remains of Wili.iam Hari, Db Warren, ami Guniireka, his W ife, the Daughter of VVii.uiam the Conquf.ror On Tuesday morning, as the workmen employed by the Brighton, Lewes, and Hastings Railway Oompanv were removing the earth in the Priory grounds at Lewes, their progress was arrested bv a stone, on the removal of wttich they discovered two cists or cottins side by side. On the lid of one was the word ' Gundreda," perfectly legible, and on the lid of the other " Willns " On removing the lids the remains appeared quite perfect, and the lower jaw of William Earl de Warren in extraordinary preservation. The cists in which the bodies were deposited were not more than three feet in length, and about two feel wide, and there is no doubt that they had been removed from some other place, and re interred : and ac cording to tradition the bodies of William De Warren and Gundieda. his wife, were reinterred >00 years after their decease. These interesting and ancient relies were removed to Souihoven church hi which them is a verv ancient tablet to the memory of "tiundreda," and it is intended '> place the remains near this tablet. The discovery ha« produced quite a sensation in Lewes and B'lghton, and numbers have visited the place, and there is no doubt that antiquarians from all parts of the country will pay Lewes a visit to see such interesting relics'

The Iniman Bee. þÿ It is a singular sight to notice the wild apiaries of India. These melliferous insects do not, as they do in England or in cold latitudes, form their cells in the cavities of trees or in decayed edifices but construct their combs in hedge rows and on the boughs of lofty trees. The hibiscus rubifln rn appears lo be a very favourite tree wiih them, for, sometimes, from eight to nine different and distinct combs may be observed dependent from the boughs of the above elegant furniture of the forest. Hundreds of bee devouring birds may be seen lingering in the vicinage nl those nboresccnt apiaries, among others, that beautifully-plumaged jhrille, the merops apinsler, which strikes at Its victims upon the wing with surprising liacritv. Bees are never domesticated bv the natives of India ; all the honey obtained

We extract the following anecdote from an article in the current number of lienlley's Miscellany : þÿ " Never can memory he dead to the extraordinary manner in which the gallant Captain H ,of the navy, was accustomed to give vent to his mortification under his losses. He would deliberately rise Irom the table, and walk up to the fire place, over the chimney of which stood a magnificent glass. Opposite to this he would place himself, and with his shadowed portrait, hold angry and emphatic converse and remonstrance, the sulistauce reminding the shadow of the resolutions made before commencing play ; and so excited would he often become in such converse with bis other self, that he would sometimes assume menacing attitudes of pu gilisiic chastisement, and bestow on himself no very complimentary epithets, as due to his lolly and imprudence. Strange as was such conduct, it was considered but as one of the many infirmities that so peculiarly exhibit themselves in individuals, under the excitements of play. Ill tinted mirth would on sue.ii occasions lead most probably to serious results; independently of which, gentlemanly feeling would control any thoughtless outbreak. The gentleman referred lo is of high standing in society, of amiable disposition and generous heart, and universally respected."

I recollect once a hackney coach drawing up to the door, out of which got four men ; doctor, they had a gold box with them as big as that (and she held her hands nearly a foot apart, to show the size of it) containing 100,000/. in bank notes. The following is ari extract ol a letter received by the Alayor ol Clomnel, from Father Muthew ; þÿ " I have read with mingled feelings of pleasureand sorrow, a report of wlraloccurted at your late corporation meeting, on the subject of the potato crop þÿ pleasure at the proof you have given of your humanity, in offering to erect, at your expense, a farina þÿmill sorrow, that such a step is considered necessary. As I have uot a little experience respecting potato farina, you will pardon me for stating that this lurina could not be a substitute for the potato. When deprived by the process of the fibre and gluten, it is properly speaking starch, and who would propose to give even the starch of wheat as subsiantiai food to the people? The only way to pteserve the potato for food in the present emergency is to cut it into two or more slices, and to dry them on i kiln or griddle. 1 have partaken of potatos thus preserved at the Duke of Loinstei's table, and they were as well fl.i vouted at the end of a year as if fresh front the earth. H is grace always preserves a portion of his potato crop in that way. The complaint about the badness of the potato reminds me of Mr. O'Corinell's story about a hoise, whose owner complained that lie could uot fatten him, though he had tried every mode. ' Have you,' inquired his friend, 'ever tried oats?' Now, 1 would advise the trial. Oats would supply the want of the potatos. In addition to the two human bodies noticed on the gilih October (which still remain in the grasp of its ' agitated waters"), there are the bodies of two horses and a hog. These may be seen from the bank above, passing round a "funereal circuit of a mile or more in circumference, each succeeding circuit drawing litem nearer the vortex of the whirlpool, until each in its turn becomes submerged beneath the boiling element þÿ again thrown violently from its angry embrace, to repeat its former evolutions The sight of human bodies in the whirlpool is solemn and terrilic þÿ the blue waters seem to hold their prey, in defiance of human efforts to dispossess them þÿ until, satisfied in revelling with the dead, it emits them through its narrow outlet into the rapids below, to he entombed in Lake Ontario. þÿ are Toronto Globe.

Curiosity of the Chinese. þÿ The greatest curiosity was always evinced by the Chinameir to be allowed to examine our guns and the mechanism of our locks ; but so great was the contrast between their rusty and antiquated, matchlocks, and the superior workmanship of our London made guns, that they seemed perlectly helpless in the handling of the latter, and as may he supposed some truly awful misadventures were the consequence. One poor fellow, who was not content with examining the outside, must needs peep down the barrels to see how beautifully they were polished, and in so doing he contrived to let off the gun at the same time, which literally carried away the whole of Ins face, killing him upon the spot. Upon atiothei occasion one of our Chinese attendants, whom we had engaged to assist us in heating for game, led by curiosity to examine one of the officer's guns which was leaning against the thwarts of a boat from which we tiad just landed, contrived to shatter the thigh of one of It s comrades in so dreadful a manner that his life was only saved by immediate amputation. Nor were the accidents which might affect the lives of the Chinamen, or even ourselves, the only reason for our determination not to allow again arty of our guns to come within the reach of these native attendants : as upon one occasion, and not very long after the two dreadful accidents just related, another misfortune occurred to two Englishmen. These two sportsmen had been spending the morning shooting near the

coast, and after having placed their guns, ammunition, game, tfcc, in a boat, wluch they had hired from a Chinese fisherman for the purpose of conveying ihem home, they turned back to a cottage not many yards distant, to get something which they had left, but how great was their surprise and mortification to discover, upon their immediate return, that the rascally boatman had taken the opportunity of decamping with the whole of their guns, game, and other treasures! þÿ nor did they ever recover them, or hear to what part of the country they had been taken. þÿ I'll' twin's Sportin g 1 Ingatine.

THE IVORY CRUCIFIX. From l-lte American Review. A True work of \rt. þÿ There is now in ibis citv, brought over from Italy by the American Consul at Genoa, a more exquisite and noble work o ! art than lias probably been in this country. It is a Christ on the Cross, wrought out of a single piece of ivorv by a Genoese monk. 1 fie circumstances attending its execution and disposal and the character of the monk by whom it was worked are of singular interest. Passing one evening near the old convent of St: Nicholas, which stands on the semicircular hill that sweeps around back of Genoa þÿ an immense picturesque building, at one time used for barracks try Napoleon, now half in ruins ami tenanted by a few old monks þÿ Mr. L. found one ol those strange þÿo clock intellectual beings, peculiar to the Catholic Church. His account of the origin and progress ol his sacred work was extraordinary, and entirely in keeping with such a character. There had been in some garret or store house of Genoa, for years, eentuiies perhaps, longer, at least, than any one had remembered, or heard þÿ an immense block ol ivory, ol a strange appearance It was much larger than anv piece that had ever been seen, being in a seamless solid beam, over three feel long, fourteen inches in diameter, and weighing more than one hundred and twenty live pounds. All the antiquarians in Italy who have looked at it, have pronounced it a relic of the antediluvian world, no modern piece of ivory being at all to be compared with it either in size or appearance. It w as

supposed to have been brought from the East in some Genoese vessel when that stale w is famed for her maritime enterprise, and had ships in all parts ol the world. It was looked upon, however as useless, except for a curiosity of unknown origin the whole exterior being thoroughly discolored and decomposed, and the decay apparently reaching the centre. From some indications, the monk is induced to think otherwise. He feels himsclt moved with a sacicd impulse. Heaven has provided þÿ marvellously þÿ a substance for the image of the divine Christ. It must indeed he made, by exceeding skill and toil, such as was never seen. Ii was necessarv first to remove the decayed portions. The outside was found to lie cd a dull gruv, and porous ; the parts next to this were denser, and of a dark mottled brown; then deepened into a substance black as ebony, and nearly as hard as glass ; between this there was nearly an inch thick, almost, as hard hut of a curdled yellow. Having with great labor cut all this away much of it being almost impervious to instruments of steel a solid mass þÿ ef ivory was reached, of a pu e cream color, entirely unchanged bv the action ol centuries, measuring about thirty three inches in length and eight inches diameter, in and weighing about eighty pounds. From tins substance, which could with difficulty he mil, but slowly etched and scraped a wav, the crucified Christ was to he wrought The account which the monk of St Nicholas gave of his long labour up to
the time Mr. L. entered his unfrequented cloister, was simple auii ailecting. He knew .

nothing, by practice, ol the shaping wt images; he had never wrought upon a piece of ivory in his life. But he thought the dear Lord and gracious Mary Mother would aid him in so holy a labor. He would he inspired to make a divine work. And suddenly, he said, the inspiration came þÿ like a l.iOug'A. A vision sprung up within him þÿ (he did not know that thus the ideal always arises to genius !) He saw Christ on the þÿcross dead. it never could pass away from him, and he knew it was sent to him for the holy image he must make. Always, therefore, day and night, he prayed before that crucified vision iri his soul, while he began confidently to give it form from the hard beam ol ivory that lay constantly before him. It became to him a work of devotion and sublime hope. With such patience arid severe enthusiasm the Monk of St. Nicholas had been now nearly four years engaged upon the statue of Christ when Mr. L. visited him. He was very much worn vvitti his constant toil, and what was more, the restless cxciternei t of a naturally vivid mind ; but the high, pale forehead, and the eyes glowing and thoughtful, though deeply sunken, spoke at once the intellectual capacities of the man. i he worn was so far completed as to show at a glance its remarkable character. tation, he accepted the offer, and Mr. I,, had him carry the statue at once to the consulate residence, where he came frequently, for six months longer, to give :t the last touches.

The Kroomen are indispensable in carrying on the commerce and maritime business of the African coast. When a Krooboat comes alongside, you may buy the canoe, hire the men at a þÿmoment s warning, and retain thorn in your service lor months. They expend no lime or trouble in providing their equipment, since it consists merely of a »uaw hat and a piece of while or coloured cotton gilded about their loins. In iheir conoes, they deposit these girdles in the crowns of theii Inis: nor is it unusual, when a shower threatens them on shore, to sec them place this sole garment in the same convenient receptacle and then make for shelter. When rowing a boat, or paddling a canoe, it is their custom to sing; and, as ihe music goes on, they seem to become invigoþÿ rated. applying iheir strength cheerfully, and with limbs as unwearied as their voices. þÿ One of their number leads in recitative, and the whole company respond in the chonis - The subject of the song is a recital ol the exploits ol the men. their employments, their intended movements the news of the coast, and the character of their employers. It is usual, in these extemporary siiains, for the Kroomen attached to a man of war to taunt, with good-humoured satire, lie ir friends who arc more laboriously employ l in merchant vessels, and not so well fed an I paid. Their object in leaving home, and ciitenng into the service of navigators, is generally to obtain the means ol purchasing

wives, the number of whom constitutes a man's importance. The sons of ' þÿgentlemen1 (for there is such a distinction of rank among them) never labour at home, hut do not hesitate to go away, for a year or two, and earn something to take to their families. On the return of these wanderers þÿ not like the prodigal son but bringing wealth to their kindred þÿ great rejoicings are instituted. A bullock is killed bv the head of the family, guns are fired, and two or three days are spent in the performance of various plays and dances. þÿ The þÿ þÿboy gives all his earnings to his father, aud places himself again under the parental authority. The Kroomen ofn.aturer age, on his return from an expedition cl this kind, buys a wife, or perhaps more than one, and distributes the rest of his accumulated gains among his telativts. In a week, he has nothing left but his wives and ins house. Age is more respected by the Africans than by any other people. Even ii the son he 40 years old, lie seldom seeks to emancipate himself from the paternal government If a young man tails in love, he, in the hist place, consults his father. The latter makes propositions to the damsel's father, who, il his flaugliter agrees to the match, announces 'he terms of purchase. The price varies in different places, and is also influenced by other circumstances, such as the respectability and power of the family, and the beauty and behaviour of the girl. The arrangements here described are often made when the girl

is only live or six years of age, in which case she remains with iier friends until womanhood, and then goes to the house of her bridegroom. Meantime her family receive the stipulated price, and are responsible for good behaviour. Should she prove faithless, and run atv tv. her purchase money must he rclu. ded bv tier friends, who, in their turn, have a ei.tun Upon the family of hint who seduces or harbours her- If prompt satisfaction he not made (which, however, is generally the c ine, there will he a þÿ big þÿpalaver, and a much heavier expense for damages and costs. It, after the commencement of married life, the husband is displeased with his þÿwife conduct, s he complains to her lather, who either takes her hack, and repays the dowry, or more frequently advises that she he flogged. In the latter alternative, she is tied, stnived, and severely beaten: a inode of conjugal discipline which generally produces the desired effect. Should the wile be suspected of infidelitv, the husband may charge her with it, and demand that she drink the poisonous decoction ot sassy wood, which is used as the test of guilt or innocence, in all cases that are cons.dered too uncertain for human judgment If her stomach free itself from the fatal draught by vomiting, she is declared innocent, and is taken hack by her family, without repayment of the dower. On the Other hand, il the poison begin to take effect, she is pronounced guilty ; an emetic is administered in the shape of common snap; and
tier husband may, at bis option, either send her home, or cut off her nose and ears.

On the 15th, the Gortes were opened. þÿ The following is the Queen's Speech : þÿ and which ever Gentlemen, Senators ami Deputies. During the short space of time that has elapsed sitlce the termination of the last session of the Oortes no remarkable alteration has taken place in the relations of my kingdom with the other powers. The negotiations pending with the Holy See continue. During that interval the ratifications of the treaty concluded with the Emperor of Morocco have been exchanged, as well as those of the treaty of reconciliation, peace and friendship with the Republic of Chili An unexpected accident has prevented the conclusion of the same formality with respect to the treaty recently agreed upon with the Rupublic of Venezuela. It goes against us to treat even with momentary levity anything that concerns such an awful calamity as war, and the further destruction of human life, or we should feel inclined to aay that two can play at that game ; and that it is as open to us as to them to fill our dock with war sieamers. Our readers have been made aware of our desire and our purpose, the subject having been fairly taken in hand by both Houses of Congress, to ref rain from any further discussion on the merits of the Oregon ques turn From that purpose we shall not now depart though strongly templed to do so. It has, however, become our duty to put our readers, and especially those engaged in commercial and maritime pursuits, (and therefore most likely to be aflected by a change in the present prosperous circumstances of the country.) upon their guard against too great a reliance upon our predieatior.s, by stating that recent occurrences have shaken the confidence which we have heretofore expressed in the peaceful termination of the Oregon controversy. Our avowed confidence in a peaceful termination of the controversy was founded upon a conviction, derived from the Annual Message of the President of the United Xiaies, (taiving all its parts together) I hat he looked foi a pacific result, which we do not doubt tie still expects. This confidence was fortified by the information which lias readied this country in difierent ways, unotficial, but credible, that the British Government has anxiously desired, and yet desires to maintain peaceful relations with the United States. And when added to these considerations, we saw Mr. Calhoun, a leading member of the Democratic majority in the Senate, availing himself of the earliest opportunity after taking his seat to declare (or peace, we were fully justified in congratula-

ting our readers on the fact of so important an accession to the body of those legislators who think that peace may yet be preserved with honor, and who are not at any rale disposed to incur the hazards and horrors of war until all efforts for a pacific and honorable adjustment of the dispute shall be exhausted.

We cannot even now that the debate in the House has unsealed our eyes and shown us how near we stand to the edge of a precipice indeed, persuade ourselves that a majority in either House of Congress would, all things else being equal, prefer war to peace; hut we must confess our apprehensions that the tone of the debate in the House of Representatives, connected, as it must he, in the estimation ol all the foreign world, with the claim to þÿ ihe whole of Oregon" set up in the þÿPresident message, s cannot but be of the worst augury lor the maintenance of peace. We desire therefore to recall any expressions of confidence which we have heretofore felt ourselves authorised to use in regard to the peaceful termination of this Oregon dispute: hoping, at the same time, that counsels wiser than those which now seem in the ascendant may yet avert the dire catastrophe of war. þÿ National Intelligencer.

The Pokes. þÿ Taken separately, ihe little perspiratory tube, with its appended gland is calculated to awaken in the mind very little idea of the importance of the system to which it belongs ; but when the vast numbers of similar organs composing this system are considered, we are led to form some notion, however imperfect, of their probable influence on the health and comfort of the individual. 1 use the words þÿ imperfect þÿnotion advisedly, for reality surpasses imagination and almost belief To arrive at something like an estimate ot the value of the perspiratory system in relation to the rest of the organism, l counted the perspiratory pores on the palm of the hand, and found 3528 in a spuare inch. Now, each of these pores beirg the apertures ol a in tie tube of about a quarter of an inch long, it follows that in a square inch of skm on the palm of the hand there exists a leng'b of tube equal to 882 inches, or 73| feet. Surety such an amount of drainage as 73 1 feet in every square inch of skin, asssuming this to he the average for the whole body, is something wonderful, and the thought naturally intrudes itself, what if this drainage were obstructed l Gould we need a stronger argument for enforcing the necessity of attention to the skin ? On the pulps of the fingers, where the ridges of the sensitive laver of the true skin are somewhat finer than in the palm of the hand, the number of pores on a square inch a little exceeded that of the palm ; and on the heel, where the

ridges are coarser, the number of pores on the square inch was 22tJ8. and the length of tube 567 inches, or 47 feet. To obtain an estimate ol the length of tube of the perspiratory system of the w hole sot face of the body, 1 think that 2800 might be taken ns a fair average of the number of pores in the square inch, and 700. consequent I v, of the number of inches in length. Now, the number of square inches oi surface in a man of ordinary height and bulk is 2500 ; the number of pores, therefore, 7,000.000, and the number of inches of perspiratory tube 1,750,000, that is, 145,833 feet, or 48,000 yards, or nearly 28 miles Wilson on the shin.

VVe find the following in a þÿGraham Town s (Cape ol Good Hope) journal, just received : þÿ þÿGraham T s own was visited on Thursday evening, the 16ih ol October, by a severe thunderstorm, which was very near being attended with most calamitous results. 1 he lightning, at each discharge, instead ol being instantaneous, appeared to be a continuous stream of electricity pouring down lor an appreciable interval of time, and leaving behind it a faint streak of white light, whilst the simultaneous crash of the thunder was terrific. The electric fluid struck several times in different parts of the town, and at half past six a broad stream ol light was observed to descend behind the Drolsdy Barrack, accompanied by a deafening peal of thunder. This, it was afterwards ascertained struck the powder magazine, containing about 60.000 lb. of gunpowder, besides large quantities of shells, rockets, ball cartridges, &,(; The lightning first struck the gable end on the eastern side of t fie building facing the town, where the fluid separated, one slientn passing directly downwards leaving a black sneak on the wall inside the þÿmagazine. -the other branching oil lo the porch, shattering the wall m seveial places and tearing off a portion ol the dour post. The sentry, who was at a distance of about 40 feet from the spot where the lightning struck, was thrown

to the ground aud remained in a state of Insensibility for an hour and a hall. If the electric fluid iiad stiuck a few feel further to the westward on the ridge, there is eieiv reasou to believe that the magazine would have exploded, and the whole of the upper part of the town have been laid in ruins It is said that in consequence of the east wall being rather damp the powder was removed from actual contact with it son e short time ago, and that perhaps to this circumstance, and to the fact of the damp wall conducting the electricity more readily into the eatth, our providential escape may be þÿattributed.

Cask Making by Machinery þÿ Considerable sums of money have al various times been expended in trying to bring to perfection machinery for making casks, but heretofore this object has been unattained, some parts always having to be finished by manual labour. A very ingeniously constructed machine for making casks by machinery has been constructed by iMr. W. Wild, of Bedfordstreet, Broughton road. The lags or staves, hoops, and heads are in the first instance dressed otf bv other machinery which is being constructed for the purpose; afterwards the finishing machine is fed with the previously prepared heads, hoops, and staves, and will in two þÿminutes time turnout a complete barrel, vastly superior in Workmanship to what has hitherto been efiecled by manual labour. Old barrels can also as easily be repaired by the same machine, the only difference in tune being occupied in the taking to pieces of t fie old barrels previously to substituting such flesh staves, heads, or hoops, as may be required previously to feeding the machine. The barrels, when completed, are vastly superior to any heretofore turned out by manual labour, the machine fitting each stave as close as though the wh le barrel had been foi med of one piece of limber, thus doing away with the necessity when made by hand of tilling up any defects with rushes, which ( Ian it is well known has the effect of rendering casks very foul, unless extraordinary cate he taken, and consequently much time is occupied in

thoroughly cleansing them. þÿ Manchester Co uriei . T I THE IS AVAL OFFICER ON HOARD THE WEST INDIA STEAMERS. This officer is termed the Admiralty agent and although he is much among us, the precise nature or extent of his duties is not very generally known. The following outline therefore from an undoubted source may therefore not be unacceptable to the public ; The Admiralty Agent is always a Lieutenant in the Royal Navy, and receives his appointment from the Admiralty, as its Agent to watch the fulfillment ol the contract on the part of the Company to the Government. To this end a minute journal of the proceedings of the steamer ; particularly ot her sailings and arrivals, is kept ; all injuries of hull, or machinery, or insufficiency of crew, equipment, boats, &o , or any other circumstance, that would either cause delay or danger in conveyance of the public mails, is noted. þÿ From this source these separate reports are sent every fifteen days to the Admiralty. General Fost Office, and to the Admiral commanding on the West India Station. Thus tiie state of every steatvvr is known at very short intervals to her Majesty's Government, that it may enforce a prompt remedy, should any be required. This officer is tltus at once an impoiianl guarantee for the safe state of the steamer, an i a check upon delays or irregularity, and li presence must necessarily give an unbounded confidence to passengers embarking in them. It is also his duty to report all ships of War seen of any nation, with their movements, to the Admiral and senior Officers, and also to the government, so that

it is incessantly aware of anv naval force being in the track of those vessels : as well as of any sudden political movement that may come to the officer's knowledge. To these duties is annexed the charge of the public mails, which are frequently of great importance for the immense amount in hills contained within them. He has them simply sealed in his charge (but he has nothing to do whatever with individual letters, nor is a hag un boatd to deposit them, as it is generally supposed, but lie has the power to prevent letters being conveyed except through the medium of the Mail and Fost tJllice.) The delivery ami receipt of the mails is frequently one that in its execution require s nerve, from the state of the weather and the nature of the landing places. On one route tu the course ofa few days fifty landings and embarkings are necessary, and this officer's boat being swamped is by no means uncommon. One of the steamets boats lately was placed, blowing heavily at midnight, oir Anti;ua, in the most perilous circumstances, the Bishop and his daughter being in it, and the same ship's boat was upset by a squall off St. Lucia, and the Admiralty Agent and crew being bv the greatest chance rescued, alter struggling on her bottom some time þÿ And at certain times of the vear the landing on the Coasts of the islands is very critical and dangerous, and the shores of Tampion, Puerto Rico, Nassau, Ghagres, ami the frequent and droarv falls and night landings amidst heavy surfs, are duties that might hide

from general observation, hut lull wiihin the sphere of this officer's duties. He is totally distinct Iroin the Company þÿ is paid by, and is the only officer employed by, the Government on board the steauiet ; at once evinc-

e m o i iz at i a ing the judgement of bet Majesty's Government in placing a competent, disinterested, arid independent officer on board of them to ensure the efficacy of the ships, and responsible from his na-al position, for the public correspondence placed in his charge.

Mr. Whitney, whose return from a tour of ex, juration in the far West, was noticed some weeks since, is preparing to urge upon Congress his magnificent project of a Rail Road from Luke Michigan to the Fucilio Ocean, lie lias published an Address to the Fnuple of the United States, explanatory of his de. igu, ol the means ot its accomplishment. and of the gieat results which may he expected from it " It is my desire," he says in his address " to call your attention parti cularlv to t1 liemorial here annexed, and also the Report from the Committee on Roads and Canals; you will there see that I ask lor do miles wide of land front the Lake to the Facdin Ocean \uu will also see exph. I led some ot the great tesults to be produced from this work. You will see that it will change the whole world, and \ou will see tl.at each one and all of you have the power without cosi m puce to do more than all mankind hefnie v ou have done þÿ 1 he lauds which I a-k are yours; all I ask is you is and tools to give 1 ask riot for mv seif, bui i ash loi yon, that you mnv bv vour simple as nt d" itn.t wl ich shall he handed down to i >e remotest period of time as the gre. ; est, e the most magnificent work of all ages ami ol all time. A work which will bring the vast world together as one nation, one family ; a work which shall allow us to traverse the vast globe in 30 days ; a work which must civilize and christianize all mankind ; a woik whivli must place us in the

centre of the world ; Lurope on the one side, and \sia and Africa on the other, compelling ail fvirope to pass through us to Asia and Africa : influencing all mankind, bringing all under our glorious and happy influence of freedom and independence. 1 ask it for you, for your children, and for the world. J ask it that our destiny as a nation may be ac com pi i. shed " Mr. Whitney estimates the cost of the road, at $20.0(10 per mde for tiie whole distance of some 2100 utiles. The proceeds of tue lauds granted, sixiv miles wide along the route of the road, are to tie applied to the const ruction of the road, under the superintendence of commissioners to be appointed by the G ivernment. The lands to be sold as the wot k advances. Between Lake Michigan and the Missouri river, a distance of 650 miles, the lands are fertile and must be valuable. The countrv is well wooded and oilers everv facility for the construction of a railway. Beyond the Missouri for a long distance the lands are poor and without timber. Lake Michigan is therefore selected as the point of beginning because the requisite material mav he had there in abundance ; also because the value of the lands may he made at once to pay for the construction and a surplus to he applied to the cost of the work in the barren district beyond the Missouri; and for the fit rther reason that it is necessary to have a cheap and easv water communication from the Atlantic cities to transport settlers, laboreis and materials directly tu the road. This gigantic Undertaking startles a» the first view irom its stupendous magnitude þÿ Rut as one considers it and looks at it in detail the simplicity of the design becomes manifest and its practicability seems, to sav tie least, very plausible. There are already more than 2100 noles of railway in the United States þÿ probably twice as many. If these roads were all connected, as in the course of time the main routes will be, it would be an ordinary thing for a traveller to go over the whole distance. It would excite no surprise if he were to travetse the whole extent with safety and despatch. It is the idea of a single continuous route of 2400 miles which startles the imagination If it he considered as a road made up of many parts and connected at convenient points, the wonder ceases. And it is to be remembered that in the progress of events, as our settlements extend towards the Pacific, this veryconnection by rail road from the Lakes or from the Missouri to the Western Ocean, will undoubtedly made. be The question then arises why not make it now I þÿ How can the required portion of the public domain be belter appropriated? If the work is finished as proposed the result wi. he that the Government will possess the most magnificent rail way in the woild lor which ii will have paid not one dollai from its treasury ; for which it will not have levied

one dollar of tax ; lor which there will be no demands of annual dividends on the capital expended ; and upon which the charges of travel and transportation may be put so low as almost to make it a fiee road þÿ for no more revenues will be required from it than a mere sufficiency to keep it in repair and in efficient operation. It is scarcely possible that Mr. Whitney can over-estimate the important changes which the opening of this road would bring about in the commerce of the world It would place us in direct connection with the western coast of South America, with the Islands of the Facific, with Japan, with China, and the Last Indies, and would form the avenue through which would roll the traffic of eight hundred millions of people. Mr. Owen of Indiana, chairman of the committee, on Roads nod Canals in the last House of Representatives, to whom Mr. W'smemniial was referred, reported that the committee were unanimous in their opinion of the vast importance of the subject, and in their judgment, thai tt is one which well merits and ought to obtain the careful and deliberate attention of Congress, at a period of greater leisure than the present, being convinced that there are very few subjects which ofler themselves to the consideiation of Congress, that are better worth its patient and deliberate investigation. Thete is of course no impossibility of such a step. But it seems to us extremely improbable. Had it been intended by the British government to instruct Air. Pakenham to make further propositions, after t fie reception of Air. Buchanan's letter of Aug. 30, that intention would probably have been manifested previous to the session of Congress. Mr. Buchanan's letter of Aug. 30, was probably forwarded to Mr. Mc.'Lane, by the steamer of the 1st of September, but it could not have been forwarded by Mr. Pakenhani, before that of Sept. 10. This was the Caledonia, which arrived in England on the 28ih. Of course instructions founded on that communication, might have been received, and doubtless were received, by Mr Pakenham, by the Caledonia, which arrived here Oct. 10. This was six weeks beldie the delivery of the Message, during which period the negotiation was suffered to slumber. If any further movement on the part of the British government be delayed until the reception in England of tire Piesidt ni's message, they will wait until near the end of this month. Mr. Mo' Lane may have received a copy of the message by the steamer of the ad of this month, but it cannot be known to the British public until received by some vessel which sailed from this country after its delivery, probably one of the packets from New York. We shall accordingly not hear

the reverberation of the message from England until the arrival of the steamer ol Jan. 4 þÿ about the 20th of next month. We may then expect to hear the sentiments of tl<e English press upon the message, but any communications from the government upon it or the correspondence, is not to be expected till a month later, on the arrival of the 4lh of February packet, and it is doubtful whether, even then. The day of the meeting of Parliament is not yet known. It is usually about die 1st of February, but it is doubtful whether it will he early enough on the present occasion to admit of the opening proceedings, and the debate on the speech, being received by the steamer of the 4th. -mSTCStV" 3 'J Z '£ V X 2 0 IT 3

THE MINISTERIAL CRISIS. Latest Intelligence. RECALL OF Sill UOllEUT PEEL .Must of our readers will doubtless be uuprepared for the intelligence which we this day communicate to them. The attempt of Lord J. Russell to lot in a Cabinet pledged to the total and immediate abolition of the corn laws has (tiled-, and Sir K. Reel lias, at her þÿMajesty express s desire, recalled his resignation. and is now engaged in reconstructing his Cabinet. The following is the statement of the Tre asury journal, the Morning Herald ol this day, a statement which we ourselves have reason to believe to be strictly true : þÿ þÿ Her M.ijestv desired .Sir Robeit Reel to wail upon tier on Satin day, lor the purpose of linally taking leave of her Majesty. Sir Ruiaeri Reel repaired accordingly to Windsor, and on his arrival was inhumed by her M.ijestv that Lord John Russell, alter having undertaken inform a government, had tailed in accomplishing lhai task ; and that her Majesty most therefore express her desire to it Sir Robert Reel would not abandon her set vice. Sir Robert Reel informed her Majesty that, just previously to his quitting Loudon, lie had received ihe intelligence of Lord J. þÿRussell failure s ; and that, having reason to believe that those ol his colleagues who had diliered from him weie not prepared, to loim a (government, and considering that Lord J. Russell was unable to form one, he had resolved, without a þÿmoment shesitation, to withdraw Ins tender of resignation, to resume office, and to propose to parliament those measures which the exigencies ol the public

set vice might þÿrequire. The cause of the break down of Lord J. Russell was not any ddlercuce ol opinion on the subject of the corn-laws. They were unanimously doomed to a speedy extinction Matters of a purely personal nature are assigned, by those who appear to he in the seciel. to have been the cause of a failure which w i it till Ihe hearts ol the lovers ol order and ihe friends ol British Industry with gladness. The secret of the prison þÿhouse is thus related by a morning paper: þÿ It is due to the noblemen and gentlemen whose movements last week occupied so unusual a space in the columns of the public pi ess, to slate that the impossibility of constructing a ministry out of all that splendid and abundant material did not arise from any ditli rence of opinion as to the measure to he proposed. They were unanimous for an entire repeal of the corn laws and though many of the party were indisposed to take office, and not very hopeful of success, all had consented, and the business of allotting the places began. For this purpose, it is said that the species of provisional Cabinet in which the measure and the emergency had been discussed was broken op, and Lord John Russell gave separate interviews to his intended colleagues. Here, however, in the verv Inst step of his administration the Rreinier elect broke down. Rumour relates that, beginning will Lord Grev, Lord John Russell offered lorn i fie Colonial office. He accepted, but had the

curiosity to ask, who was to have the Foreign office? The answer was, Lord Ralmerston, an intimation which had the immediate effi et of neutralising Lord þÿGrey love s of place and power, patriotic and disinterested as it undoubtedly was. He most strongly objected to the appointment, and, for his ow n part, positively refused to serve with Lord Palmerston as Foreign Minister. It was in vain that Lord John represented the utter impos sibility of passing such a man bv : possibility or impossibility, Lord Grey was inexorable, and took bis ground on the absolute incompatibility of himself and Lord Ralmerston sitting at the same Council table. The whole of Friday evening is said to have been spent in fruitless endeavours to nn>ve the rock. As Lord John Russell considered that he could not dispense with either of their lordships, or at least could not afford to leave them at liberty to follow their own devices in the approaching struggle, be resolved again, tor the last time, to return his commission into her Majesty's þÿhands. Tlie following was, we understand, the intended allocation of places in the Ministry which t tie sudden resistance of Lord Grey to the appointment of Lord Ralmerston as Minister for Foreign Affairs brought to so preinatuie a close : þÿ First Lord of the Treasury, Lord John Russell. Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, Lord Ralmerston. Secretary of State for the Home Department. Sir G. Grey. Secretary of State for the Colonies, Lord Grey. Lord Chancellor, Lord Cottenhnm.

The Vice- Presidency of the Board of Trade was tendered to Mr. Cobden, an act hardlv paralleled by Ihe offer of an lush judgeship to Mr. þÿO Connell, made by the same party when previously in power. Reel will lay before parliament. We have said that of ihe precise character of that plan we cannot speak wiih full confidence; hut if we are not much mistaken, it will be found substantially to be þÿ somewhat like the following ; þÿ It will Sc moved, we think, in a set of resolutions, which will, perhaps, not exceed five in number. In the first, the ex- Premier will most probably slate the principle upon which the sliding-scale was proposed, and call upon ihe house to affirm its success during everv vear down to the present, witetr circumstances totally unforeseen, and beyond the i.uulrol of human counsel, have occur i ed

and have thus produced (as he will allege) an exigent necessity for revising and modifying the system. In the second resolution, he will state the failure of the potato crop, and the concurrent defident harvests on the Continent ; the conquest actual and further apprehended suffering of the Irish poor: the certain pressure upon the English corn market. and the reasonable apprehension that the produce of the late harvest (unassisted bv foreign importation) will be insuflicient for the supply of the kingdom during the latter months of the summer. In the third resolution, he will probably state that the population of the kingdom is annually increasing by a certain given and admitted amount, and that as the acreable extent of land admitting of cultivation cannot be increased in the same proportion, or indeed at all increased, it has become an indisputable fact that we must not only annually be supplied with corn 'bom abroad, but that such foreign importation must be increased from year to year; and that in order to meet the actual necessities of the kingdom, such supply must be rendered certain, and for this end and object must be relieved, as much as possible, from all future restriction. The fourth resolution will propose the plan of repeal. The fifth will enumerate the proposed compensations, namely, such a revision of our system of taxation, and particularly of that part of it which presses upon land þÿ such a? the hop duty, the malt tax. the poor- rates, the county rates þÿ as may

lead to the consideration of what burthens may be so removed, mitigated, or rendered ntore equal amongst different classes, so as to compensate the landed interests for sacrifices required for tfie public good

PORTUGAL. \ Royal decree has been published amend, ing the sanitary law of the 18th of September, 1844, which caused so much dissatisfac tion at the time, and has continued to do so ever since. The amendments from which foreign shipping derive benefit are as follows, viz; þÿ 1. Eoreign vessels sailing from Portuguese ports are no longer obliged to go to the useless expense of taking bills ol health. y. The health visit on vessels of one or two masts is to be 4800 reis, and on threemasted vessels 7200 reis; hut as the sums paid on this account are to be compensated by a corresponding deduction from the tonnage dues, the charge for t he health visit becomes in reality merely nominal. 3. Vessels bound to Portugal and provided with hills of health from the Portuguese consul at the port of departure, or from the local authorities should there he no Portuguese Consul there, are not obliged to renew their till of health or get it endorsed at any inletmediate port they may touch at, unless they stay tnore than eight days at such intermediate port. 4. The maximum of quarantine on vessels with suspected or foul lulls of health is reduced to two thirds of its former duration.

Extraordinary Fortitude. þÿ The Edinburgh Weekly Chronicle narrates the following extraordinary instance of piescnce of mind and fortitude. A few days ago, Samuel Mason, tentor in one of Mr. þÿSwan s mills near Kukaldy, met with a severe accident in the following manner; þÿ Having observed a cord entangled with one of t he belts, he went up a ladder to relit- ve the same: but, on doing so, the slack portion of the coid took a turn round his left thumb and arm as was drawn onward by the movement of the Being thus fixed, he foresaw his in-

stant destruction if drawn tip to the pullev by the l e t, and, with singular fortitude and \ iesence of mind, be giasped a column close bv with his arms and legs, and field on till Ins arm was literally sawn and tom asunder; being thus relieved, he slid down the column to the floor, took off his bonnet and clapped it on the bleeding stump, holding it with his hand, rushed out, and across the street to his father in law, where, exhausted and breathless, he fell on t lie floor, before the engine was set off, being the first means by which anv assistance could have been rendered him. An express was immediately dispatched fi>r surgical aid to Kirkaldy, a distance of more than tvvo miles, when his arm was amputated above the torn part ; hut, finding t he bone so much injuied, they made another amputation a little below the shoulder joint Me stood tin opeiations well, though he must have been much exhausted from the loss of blood and the unavoidable length of lime that elapsed before surgical assistance could he rendered. Nevertheless, after being carried to his own house in a chair, he went up stairs on his feet, and has since been doing wonderfully well.

New Stereotyping Process. þÿ We had the satisfaction of seeing, on Satuiday last, at the office of Mr. Hugh Wilson, lithographer and engraver, Trongate, a new patent process ol stereotyping, which, for simplicity, and, above all, the celerity of its execution, bids fair, at no distant day, to number the present system with the things that were. The old process, which was undoubtedly one of the greatest improvements ever grafted on the ait of typographer, consists, as our readers may be aware, in taking impressions from forms or pages of moveable type, hy means of

stucco, which, when dried and prepared, boms the matrices þÿI oi stereotype plates. 1'lie process, however, is tedious, requiring careful picking, placing, oiling, and preparing. In the new mode the progress is completed, as it were, in u handclap. In taking the tin pressiou, stucco is entirely dispensed w ih: and, instead of it, a piece of damped, prepared card board is placed over the surface of the page ol moveable type, and an impression beat out of the type into the card, by repeated

strokes of a hard þÿbrush a unit of the operation, w hich according to the size of the page, occupies about a minute and a h If This card, which now answers the purpose of a matrix, is dried and inserted in an iton frame with a moveable top. or surface, constituting a mould, which has been previously heated to an equable temperature. The lid is then brought .down, the mould shifted by a hinge from the horizontal to the perpendicular, and the liquid metal poured into the matrix by a small orifice which has been left, and in a minute the stereotype page is pronounced complete. At least, the only preparation for the press which it requires, is the trimming of the superfluous edges, which is done by a circular saw with great celerity The back of the plate is as smooth as the slab of metal from which it receives its impression and thus the platting process in stereotyping is now done away. The young French workman, whom we observed conducting the process at Mr. Wilson's, informed us that the whole operation, from beginning to end, was conducted in less th in an hour, while the ordinary period of taking siereoty pe casts is, we believe, from ten to twelve hours, liable to the breaking, þÿsn iiting or warping oi the stucco matrices þÿ tisks which are unknown in the new card process. During the half hour that we remained, the operatives " heat þÿin impressions from a card of steamboat advertisements, and also a page from the (Missionary Intelligencer types which had been borrowed from a print-

ing office at random þÿ and produced plates from them a« distinct and clear as any we have ever seen to issue from a stereotyping establishment. We may add, that many impressions þÿ so many indeed as a dozen þÿ may he taken from the same card ; and the process is one of such perfect clearness, that a man might almost work at it in a pat lor. in his dress coal. We hail (lie new mode with satisfaction, as one which will materially aid and abet in the cheapening and extension of kn< w ledge. þÿ i C lasgow Jim aid.

from Bell's Weekly Messenger, London, December 1, 1845. Foreign Inteluigence. þÿ The foreign in telligence of tbe week is of no importance whatever. The French papers, having no immediate grievance of their own, are very kindly occupied in giving advice to our ministers and Cabinet, and all this advice is most characteristically marked with the peculiar qualities of the gentlemen from whom it proceeds. Cunning, managing, equivocating, anti as some will have it false and double dealing, as some of the measures of Sir U. Feel are by these persons openly stated to be, it appears that the English minister is still Hot sufficiently cunning and equivocating lor them. They call tins system consummate policy, and true prudence, and congratulate England upon having such a minister. Ac cording to them. Sir R: Feel is only watching his time to make a grand sacrifice ol the Conservatives for the public good, nnd by some master stroke to deceive them into the blind sufferance of a course of policy which will þÿeventually save them. According to them, it is the present object of Sir If. Feel to fuse all parlies into a moderated Whigism, and to compose what they call a juste miheu, or a þÿ terium medium quid.'' very much in the same mode in which þÿ1 jiiglishmenmake brandy and water þÿ something which spoils the brandy, and does not improve the water.

France. þÿ The French papers are chieflv occupied with two topics ; the utility of their laige steam fleet in ihe event of a war with Russia, and the probable measure of Sir R. Feel to relieve and conciliate Ireland. Under Ihe air of friendly suggestions, they bit Sir Robert with many hard blows. They charge him with having obtained place as a Tory minister, and now exercising his power in carrying Whig measures. According to these Frenchmen, Sir Robert has persuaded the horse to let him mount him, that by his aid he might hunt down the wolf, their common enemy, and having at first done the horse some little service in this wav, that he has now in turn made a league with the wolves, and that its main stipulation is that both shall use the horse as a common victim- According to these gentlemen he has enlisted his Conservative friends os crimps enlist men for the African and East Indian service ; he has induced them to enlist by false promises and cunning deceits, and having enlisted them, he bids them escape if they can from the meshes of martial law and the articles of war. With the usual morality ol French editors, Sir Robert is praised to the skies for the dexteritv of his conduct. Upon the other topic, that of their large steam navy, though Russia is the kingdom against which they anticipate this navy will be so useful, we rather presume that England is the one intended : if so the ready answer to their hoast is. that wc as well as they can build these steam vessels, and that in the presence of an
English navy a flotilla of steam- vessels at Boulogne would be as harmless as were the flat bottomed boats of Napoleon. þÿ Ibid November 24.

LjIiuption of Mount Hecla. þÿ According lo news received froin Iceland to lite 12th of October, the eruption of Mount Hccla still continued with the same violence, the lava ran from the south west crater without intermission, and had already covered a space of three miles, and heaped up a mass in plain a at the foot of the mountain 30 to 40 cubits in height. This river of lava presented on a clear night a spectacle at once magnificent ami imposing. Let the reader picture to himself a river of fi lming fire precipitating itself from the summit of a lofty mountain, and assuming as it advances from the crater a redder colour, or a sort of bluish red. þÿ Three immense columns of smoke constantly ascended from the three craters which had formed and spread themselves over the surrounding districts. Up to this period the lava had not destroyed tint hum, hut the ashes which had fallen into the meadows had already exercised most pernicious clients upon the cattle, especially the cows. In some districts as many as 40 had perished. Tito pastures in the district of liangnrvalla; situate to the eastward of Heehi, were entirely devastated on t lie first eruption hv considerable quantities of pumice stone, and it is feared that a great number of sheep perished on the occasion Much uneasiness is felt at the duration of the eruption, as 'he lava, when it ree< ives fresh supplies, alwavs approaches nearer to the cultivated lands.

A Mttutixar. in Brittany. þÿ "In the neighbourhood of Quimper, the innriiugeceremonies are singular, and some- what burlesque. The village tailor hears a most prominent part on these occasions. He appears in ilritiauy greatly to resemble the barber of the old French comedy. Frequently deform ed hi a person, and (owing, no doubt lo his sedentary occupation) he is a gossip, a gobetween, a poet: the favourite of the wo men, whose repasts lie shares, and the ridicule of the men. It is not, perhaps, generally known, that in Brittany the females of a family dine after and apart fiom their m do relations: indeed, nowhere is the inferi oritv of women inure strongly expressed and dwelt upon, nowhere is her subjection greater, ban among the Breton peasantry.
