T» JL « c 'J t> i A'n s. mai tinge the lender luloiement may he used in speaking to the bride; aftei the wedding day, tins endearment censes, to give way to a more reserved and despotic foim of address, as if marriage were too serious to retain any of the fnvolities of love, and the woman was to learn at once that all equality between her and her partner was at an end for ever. þÿ When a Breton peasant has marriage in view, he charges the tailor to visit the young woman, who always refers him to her pa rents; and, if their reception of his proposal is favourable, he returns to his employer þÿ The tailor then, hearing in his hand a branch ol the genet, or broom, from which, like our I'lantagenets, he derives Ins name of Bazvalen, (baguette de genet,) and dressed in a singular manner, wiilt one stocking red and one purple, accompanies the young man and his nearest relative to the bride's house While the parents arrange mere worldly matters, the young couple are allowed an hour of un inteirupted conversation; after which, hand in hand, they approach the table round which their relatives and the important Bazvalen aie altendy seated- The young couple eat with the same knile, and drink with the same glass, and aie considered finances. A day is appointed for a meeting of boilt families, which always takes place at the bride's house, ami is called the villaden, or the beholding þÿ On this occasion the young girl appears in her gayest attire, her scaiiel boddir.c, wiih worked eyelet holes, laced with gold or silver;

the embroidered apron, snow white cap, and all ilie finery of the Breton peasant. The young man's large bordered luit is ornament ed with ribands of several colours, and the full trousers and bright blue jacket complete Ins costume ; the jacket is often a musterpiece finery of that the tailoi's name is embroidered in coloured worsteds on the bieast, as an aitist wiites his name on a precious painting which he deems worthy of immortality. At this meeting, the farm house is in all its glory. The beds, which close with doors like wardrobes, aie resplendent wiih wax and rubbing; the rafters are hung with hams; the old black coffers you always see in Breton houses disclose their riches; linen, lace, counterpanes, blankets, all the wealth of the family, are displayed ; and horses anil cattle are inspected. Above all, the bee hives are decorated with scarlet and yellow ribands, for the bees are supposed to he parlieulatly tenacious of respect, and if they are not put into mourning at a death, and adorned in token of rejoicing for all fortunate occasions, they immediately lake flight, choosing to he treated as the friends and confidants of the family they enrich by their labours, or certainly punish ingratitude by to desertion. As soon as the day marriage of is fixed, w hich is generally about a week after the celladen, the young girl, accompanied by her bridesman or garcon d'honneur, and the youug man by his bridesmaid, go with a white slick in their hands from door to door, inviting to the wed-

ding. The invitation given verse, is in setling forth ihe period of the mariiage, the place appointed and the name of the aubergisle or traiteur who provides the dinner. þÿ at the Sometimes 000 to 800 persons assemble on these occasions, and seldom less than 300 or 400: and as no guest goes empty handed, hut all take presents of flax, corn, honey, and sometimes of money, these gifts form a material addition to the resouiees of the young house keepers; and many people marry with hut little more than these friendly eontribu lions and their own labours to rely on for subsistence." þÿ The Keepsake.

Death ok a Sinoui.au (Jha'imteh. þÿ Christian Urban, first alto of the It \ nl Academy of Music, expired at Paris last week. He was a consummate musician, and highly esteemed in the musical world. Short, ill shaped, invariably wearing a sky blue coat, and dining every day at the same table at the Cafe Anglais, Urban was well known for his originality. But what above ait distinguished him was an extreme devotion, the minute practices of which he scrupulously followed He went to mass every day of the week, and on Sundays attended every service. At night, he brought with him to the opera orchestra pious books which he read whenever he was permitted to quit ins bow for a moment. You will ask why so devout an artist had engaged at the opera. He deplored it, but had been obliged to enter the band. Urban had at first devoted his talents lo sacred music, but it had not yielded him enough to live upon, and necessity had thrown him into the dramatic world a theatrical musician. All the resources of his mind were employed in reconciling his ideas wiih ihe exigencies of his profession. Whilst accompanying with his violin the song and the dance, he had remained a complete stianger to the spectacle, and to its pomp arid fascinating attractions. He had made it a rule to- keep his head constantly bent on his chest, and his eyes lowered on his music or prayer book. On no account, would he have infringed the duty lie had imposed on himself for the slightest infraction would have been to him an enormous sin. Never did his eyes

venture across the proscenium We do not evaggeiate; it is literally true that Christian Urban was many years in the Opera orchestra, without ever having seen the stage. He was as unacquainted with the cantahicet as with the dansetises. One day, in a drawing room, he met a young and pretty woman, who addressed liirn as a person whom one often sees, and complimented him on his talents in tlaitering terms. " Who is that ladv ?" asked Urban. " What, don't you know her ?" replied the master of the house. " I have never seen her." " Impossible ! look at her well." " In vain do I lo -k at her," reiterated Urban. " I assure you that I hae never seen Iter before." He told the truth, and it was necessary to nante Madame Dolus. whom lie actually saw for the first time, although he had heard her sing for the last 10 years. Urban knew no faces on the opera stage, and knew as little of the piavs as of the performers. Several modern woiks have exhibited on the stage the ceremonies and pomp of the Church Urhan considered it a profanation, and shuddered when he heard the chorus utter church music. One evening, whilst a procession moved across the stage, he was seen to kneel in the orchestra, cross himself, and pray w ith joined hands as if he had been at Notre Datnc. At the moment death struck him, Urban was about to retire on a pension, and devote himself to monastic life. He has died, leaving the reputution ofn very intelligent man, who during 25 years never missed a single performance

opera, and never saw Guillaume, Tell, Hubert le Diablo., the Huguenots, the Juice, Sylpliide, nor Giselle þÿ of a musician ol t e opera hand who was faithfully at his | o.-t every night duiing lltr.se 25 years, mid wlm, though provided with cxicllent eyes, never saw Aldlles Falcon, Nourrit, Tagiioni, Mdmc. Stollz Dtiprrz. Carlotta Grisi. or any other of the gods or goddesses of ciil cr song or ballet. þÿ Put ts Punt November 1845.

þÿ ht©Z»- The O'Connell Hunt. þÿ The wickedness of collecting money for O'Connell at n season like the present has struck with astonishment one of his most ardent admirers, the Paris Presse. In speaking of the tribute, that paper says þÿ " It appears that the amount collected this year exceeds that of the past. It is inconceivable how a man who has a private income which would enable him to live in a princely manner, can have the heart to receive every year a sum of SOO.OOOf or 600,000f. extracted sous by sous from the wretched earnings of tiie poor, who cannot every day procure a meal of victuals. The population which pays this tribute is one of the most wretched of Europe, scarcely ever tasting either bread or meat, and living in dens rather than houses. Thousands of families would consider themselves fortunate if they weie treated half so well as the hounds kept by Mr. O'Connell at his manor of Derrynane Abbey. But at the present time the collection of this tribute has something particularly revolting in it. Ireland is threatened by, or rather is actually suffering from scarcity. þÿ by a wealthy mandarin. The latter regarded The potato crop, the common food of the lower orders, has in many districts completely failed : and it is at such a moment as this that Mr. O'Connell, who lacks nu luxury, permits the agents of 'the Association' to plunder those wretched creatures for the purpose of swelling his civil list. How can he expect that his adversaries should place any faith in his sincerity, and allow themselves to

be gulled when he deplores in eloquent terms the sad situation of his country T Had O'Connell, when the Protestant loids, forgetting their religious prejudices, came forward and subscribed large sums for the relief of the suffering poor, renounced the rent which lie has hitherto received, he would have acted a noble part, anil would by so doing have prov. ed to the more incredulous that his sympathy for his countrymen was capable of influencing him to make real and substantial sacrifices. To harangue for hours together in Conciliation hall is an excellent tiling no doubt, but the liish people requires something more substantial at lite present moment than his eloquence."

The Mandarin and the English lady, Nothing astonishes the Chinamen who visit our merchants at Hong Ivong so much us the deferences which is paid by our countrymen to their ladies, and the position which the latter are permitted to hold in society. The very servants express their disgust at seeing our ladies permitted to sit at table with their lords, and wonder how men can so far forget their dignity. A young English merchant recently took his youthful wile with htm to Hong Kong, where the couple were visited

the lady attentively, and seemed to dwell with delight on her movements. When she at length left the apartment, iie said to the husband, in his imperfect English. " What you give for that wifev wife yours?" " Ob," replied the husband, laughing at the singular error of his visitor, " 2.000 dollars." This our merchant thought would appear to the Chinese rather a high figure, but iic was mistaken. " Well," said the mandarin, taking out his book with an air of business, " spuse " you give her to me, I give you 5000 dollars It is difficult to say whether the young merchant was moie amazed or amused, but the grave air of the Chinaman convinced him that he was in earnest, and he was compelled, therefore, to refuse the oiler wiih as much placidity as he could assume. The mandarin was, however, pressing, and went as high as 7000 dollars. The merchant, who had no previous notion of the value of the commodity which he had taken out with him, was compelled length ul to declare that Englishmen never sold their wives alter they once came into their possession, an asset tion which the Chinaman was slow to believe þÿ The merchant afterwards had a hearty laugh with his young wife, when fie loid her that fie had just discovered her full value, as the mandaiin had offered him 7000 dollars for her. þÿ Liverpool Albion.

Affairs in tub Rio ib i.a l'i, ata. rhe position and progress of the Oregon c.ontroversv naturally engross a large share, of publi« attention ; hut there are events elsewhere which also demand heedlul notice, because their consequences, at some future time, may Uo of the first magnitude. The intelligence from Buenos Ay res which we gave yesterday, that the declaration of blockade, issued by the French and British plenipotentiaries, had been promptly followed bv a formal protest from t tit? diplomatic representative of the United States, opens a wide field for consideration and inquiry. As we have before taken occasion to intimate, the forcible intervention of France and England in the affairs of the two quasi republics lias seemed to us both unfortunate and unpistifiable. In fact we have never been able to perceive the > ight on which this system of pacific inlet vent ion, as it is called, can in aov way he justified. The pretexts set up for it are, humanity and the protection of neutral commmce. It is alleged that whenever two small powers engage in hostilities, the greater powers are under a sort ol humane obligation to step in and by main force prevent them from cutting each other's throats. Now the efficacy of this principle can in no degree fie affected by the greatness or smal'ness of the belligerents; if it applies to the minor powers it must be applicant also to the major ; if Buenos Ay res and the Banda Oriental may he stopped from lighting, so may France and England, Russia

and Austria þÿ provided theie be a power strong enough to undertake the office. Y\ e -hall not stop now to inquire how susceptible the doctrine is of support, in tiiis extent of its application, because it is sufficient lor our present purpose to cite the undisputed fact that neither Fiance nor England, Russia nor Austria, will accede to it, themselves being hvpotfieticailv the subjects of its application. It mav be observed, however, incidentally, that the principle, if thus sought to fie applied to tlie greater powers, would work incalculable mischief, and prove, perhaps, a more energetic cause of long and destructive wars than any other. The pride ed nations would at once be revolted by such an assumption, and the immediate consequence would be a renewal of that system of alliances, offensive ano defensive, which lime and again involved the whole of Europe in protracted ami bloody wars under Louis the 14th, Queen Anne, the great Frederick of I'russia, I he Uzai l'eter and Charles the 12th of Sweden If there were any one power strong enough to undertake the prohibition ol a war between Fa nee and England, for instance, the almost certain result would be an alliance of the pro bibbed powers with such others as iliev could induce to join them þÿ perhaps in fact an alliance between themselves þÿ to oppose and resi>t the dictation ; and on This quarrel they would light to the last extremity. And, as the affairs of the world are judged and managed. it would be a legitimate quarrel ; for at

the bottom ol it would lit? the dearest point of national faith and feeling, to wit, national independence and freedom of volition. But the system is contended for on the ground that t lie commerce of neutrals is impeded and broken up, ami ihciclore the own. era of that com me ice have a right to tiller-

3 'i\ Q 03 il T It 3 . pose. There might lie some shadow of validity in this plea if il were not for the fact that ninety nine times out of a hundred, commerce is more extensively injured, ami for a longer time, by the intervention than bv the war. þÿ In this very case of the South American belligerents. instance, for the war between Ibent lias been waged for several years, with great inhumanity doubtless, but with very little detriment to foreign commerce; occasional wrongs have been done, it is true, to tbo property ol neutrals, but on the whole of the war has been rather profitable to them than otherwise. The blockade of which we have just received the account puts a stop at once to all commercial operations, and in every day of its continuance will cause more loss than has at any time been caused by a whole year ol the war. And an important fact to be considered is that but for foreign intervention the war would have been ended long ago. On the part ot Montevideo it lias been sustained, for the last three or four years, almost exclusively by resident foreigners; and even they would have been subdued bad lliev bad not been repeatedly aided by the naval force ol Fiance and England. Be that as it may, however, the blockade is now declared and in force ; and our representative, doubtless under instructions from the Government, has protested against it, with a prospective reclamation tor all damages that may ensue to citizens of t fie United Sta>es. The act is important, and can scarcely fail to prove the origin, or at least

the forerunner, of a difficult controversy lierealier. In one point of view its effect may be beneficial. It establishes a precedent by winch tfie Government of the Union may be held to non-interference between belligerents half a century hence, when the Ninth Anietican republic shall he the most powerful nation on the earth, and leel itself strong enough to say that there shall fie no fighting eilhei in Europe or America. (From th e Journal des Debuts) We have teceived from Rio de Janeiro a letter, which gives some curious details relative to the working of a new diamond mine recently discovered in Brazil l'or some months past the communications and commercial intercourse with the province of Baliia have been extraordinarily brisk. A large number of inhabitants, speculators, adventurers, and even sugar planters, are emigrating with tfieir slaves to the province of Batiia, where is situate an immense diamond mine, the produce ot which is incredible. It wa» discovered in October, 1844, by a slave who in 20 days had gathered 700 carats of diamonds, and carried them a considerable distance for sale. Vrrested and imprisoned, the slave obstinately refused to disclose the locus in quo. They therefore let him loose, and put a number ot intelligent Indians upon his " trail." The latter pursued him tor several davs. and found hitti working for the extraction of the diamonds not far from Faxoeira, the second city of Baliia. investigations were then made on a large scale along a chain of mountains called Stucura, which have given the name to this mine, and on the banks of the river Puraguassu, which fails into the bay <>1 Buhia. The first persons who established themselves at the mine of Sine.ura were chiefly convicts and murderers. They made known their presence by fires and assassinations The difficulty of subsisting in the country, and the danger to which those were exposed

who proceeded thitner to exchange diamonds for the paper money ol Brazil, prevented honourable merchants front entering into the trade. By degrees, however, when tfie population had become more numerous, a system of police was established by the new colonists, and the mine was then worked upon a much larger and more extensive scale. The population, which only amounted in August, 184 1 to 8000 souls, distributed over three villages, was, at the end of July, upwards of 30,000. and on the increase. The villages at present inhabited and cultivated are seven in number, and are named þÿ Paraguas-u, f'on.bucas, Fhiqncohiqui. Fausu Boa, Andrahy, l.ancoe. The last named village, which is 20 leagues distant from Paraguassu, contains alone 3000 families and 20,000 inhabitants. The central point of the diamond trade is Paraguassu, which, although sufficiently peopled, has only at present 12 small houses ol brick- Almost all the ttiiucrs go thither on Saturdays and Sundays to sell the stones they have picked up during the week. They receive in exchange dilierent articles of consumption, arms, and apparel, which are brought thither at a great expense from I'ahia The diamonds cxitacted from Parnguassu are, generally speaking, of a brown colour, and ol a very irregular formation. White and light green, almost transparent on their first extraction from tie initio, distinguish those ol Ban toe. They are of au ooiahedul form, and arc the most in request, it i> often rcqu;»ite to dig liuoc or luui metres

in order to reach the cascaille or layer of the diamonds. Diamonds are also discovered in the rocky ravines at the bottom of the Paraguassu itself, and the streams which fall into it. The price of these diamonds varies, at Bahia, from 250 to 500 milreis per octave (07 It", to 1340f), according to their fineness and size. The octave is 17| carats : but the Brazilian carat is 7 per cent, less than the French, which makes the Brazilian eaiat about 07f. to 134f. The two English steamers of May and June brought about 5,500,000 francs' worth of diamonds from this mine. During tire months of June and July the mine yielded nearly 1450 carats per day. It is estimated to have produced, during the six months of its working, nearly 400.000 Portuguese carats (about IN 300,000 francs), of which three fifths were sent to England, another fifth to France and Hamburgh, whilst the last filth awaits buyers at llio Janeiro and Bahia' Not all the lapidaries in Europe would be sufficient to polish only one half of the produce of the Sincura nrine; thus a depreciation of that value is expected, which gives rise to the most hazardous speculations. Brazil, which has the privilege of supplying the trade 'with diamonds, did not produce annually, before the discovery of the Nineuta nnnc, more than six or seven kilogrammes, which cost more than a million for the expenses of working; thus the price, even in the rough state, has always been very high Hitherto, no very large diamonds have been found at Sincura. There 'are very few in

the world weighing more than 20 grammes. Tire largest diamond is that of Agra, weighing 1 33 grammes ; that of the Kaj ah of Matan. in Borneo, weighs 78 grammes ; that of the (jreat .Mogul, 03 grammes ; and thai ol France, called the " Kegenl," 28 grammes 89 centigrammes ; but it is of a very pretty shape and perfect ill every respect. Before being polished it weighed 87 grammes, and cost two year's labour. The mine of Sincnra presents the spectacle of an independent colony in tire bosom of the mother country. Hitherto the government has taken no steps to possess itself ol the direction of this trade, winch promises to be so abundant a source of wealth to Baton, and it will be perhaps reduced to sanction die regulations formed by the inhabitants themselves for the working of the urine, which already covers a superficies ol more than 30 leagues

From þÿHell s Weekly Messenger, London January 5, 1840. SOUTH AUSTRALIA. (Extract of a private letter ) This is a great corn as well as grazing country. Even at the present high price of \as(t;s, the farmer is satisfied with the price of 3s. per bushel, in consequence of the corn being reaped, thrashed and winnowed by a machine drawn by horses or bullocks. Till latelv, wheal has been selli' g from 2s. to 2s. 6J. per bushel. We have enormous quantities for exportation, if we could only find a market, uid if corn was admitted into Britain at the same ditty as that of Canada, it would pav our farmers to ship corn to England. We have a brisk trade with India and the adjoining colonies ; emigrants from thence, averaging twenty five per week, have been landing here lor the last twelve months. iVlanv from the other colonies would come had they the means. There is no country richer in minerals than South Australia. The iron ore is equal to anv in the world, yet no person will much it in consequence ot the richer mines of copper and lead A Captain Bagot bought eightv acres, fifty miles from this, eighteen months ago at HO/,, and has since raised hOO tons of copper ore. each ton netting at least 10/. per ton; 300 tons are slipped, the remainder ready for shipment. One hundred acres adjoining his mine wete put up by government a few weeks ago: and alter competing with a colonial company, they were purchased by Captain B igot fur 2250/. 22/ 10s. per acre. He states tint .he would not take 40 000/. cash tor the 100 acresft is calculated that he can raise (net price)

12.000/. per annum. A mme on surveyed land was taken ten davs ago, 100 acres at 160/., one third of which was immediately sold for 1000/ The government have a mineral section adjoining the Montacute mine, which all judges here consider would be purchased cheap at 10,000/ The Montacute mine, 80 acres was purchased at government auction, 12 months ago. for 1500/ Copper and lead ores are daily discovered in all parts ot the colony, hut surface mines only are saleable. Surface mines are those in which large veins or lodes of ore are seen on the smface þÿ some lodes run on the surface in a line of 10 and 20 acres. So rich and abundant is the surface ore on the government mineral section adjoining the Montacute, that 10 tons were stolen from it before discovering the thieves. It is not known when the government will put up this section. It is extraordinary that the minerals were not discovered sooner. The fact is, that in the davs of our prosperity we only surveyed and bought the richest farming lands. The first mine (lead ) two and a half miles from Adelaide, on private property, was accidental I v discovered by the wear of the drays on a road at the foot of the hills, exposing the ore buried a few inches under the soil. The first Coppermine þÿBagot was s discovered by shepherds bringing to their master the pretty curious stones, as they called them. Captain Bagot being formerly employed in an Irish copper mine, knew their value. Since these discoveries, many persons are exploring, and
numberless mines richer than those now worked are known to individuals who give

3 T, V It t> i :£ AT J 3 no information in consequence of the oiiangb in the svsiem of government sales, þÿ me regulation being sale by public auction, and the discoverers are wailing until the settlers have expended their ready money in the purchase of inferior mines before they apply to survey, and put up the richer mineral sections. You may suppose the excitement the mines are causing. i\ umbers of persons will be ruined but enormous fortunes will bemade by many. Most of the minerals are in the centre of a fanning country. Corn and cattle can be raised and fed close to the mouths of the mine. There are good roads to nearly all ol them. Cobalt, antimony, quicksilver, tfcc-, ate said to be discovered ; but the persons showing specimens will give no information. There are slight indications ot copper ore found in the wells sunk in the neighbourhood of your country section, 50 or 00 feel deep. There is nothing now to retard the prosperity of this colony: a more onetgelic or indusi i ions hodv of seniors than the South Australians does not exist; piovisions and necessaries ot every description are cheap and abundant. Large vineyards, orchards, and gardens are being formed in the colony. One colonist has a garden in North Adelaide three and a halt acres, the Iruit ot which realised last season 300/. ; and the cuttings, plants, t&c., ol Ins vines, Ne., will realise 150/. more. This gSiden iast year had the following fruits ripened: þÿ Gooseberry, currant, strawberry, raspberry, damson, several varieties of plum, Ohio cherries, ditto uecta

rules, peaches, apricots, ditto apples, ditto pears, ditto almonds, diilo tigs, ditto mulberries. quinces, pomegranates, oianges, lemons, citrons, bananas, olives, and upwards of 200 varieties of the grape. There arc: nearly 400 varieties of the grape in the garden. Melons, both water and sweet, ol every variety, sell by the cwt. from Is to 10s. and 12s The latter price is obtained at the commencement of the season. They arc: brought to town in dray loads ot a ton and more- Every variety of vegetable thrives here: they, with our fruits and corn, are more abundant and equal to any 1 have seen in England. There is an opening for industrious labour ers. Good practical miners are much want ed. Steady persons, with capital, arc certain of independence, and ol leaving a better provision tor their children than they could in Europe, 1 cannot advise the purchase of land for speculation, except mineral lands. The farming lands, commanding pasturage, runs, and surface water, are the most valuable. The runs in particular are valuable. There is no opening for professional men, except they are very clever, very steady, and possess a sum of 200/ at least to start with. A clever barrister, wiih a sound knowledge of all the branches of law, particularly conveyancing and common law, would do well. He would require a good law library, and some 300/. or 500/. to keep him going until his talents are known. There are 25 attorneys here, the earnings af all about 10.000/per annum : but there is a rich harvest in
stoic ol disputed boundaries and mining matters The above earnings have been made in our days of adversity, it is impossible to say wltal the amount was in our prosperous limes-

EFFECT OF EARTHQUAKE UPON THE MINI). We must advert to the cause of the indescribable. deep, and quiet peculiar impression which the hist earthquake we experience makes upon us, even when it is unaccompanied by subterranean noises. The impression here is not, 1 believe, the consequence of any recollection of destructive catastrophes presented to our imagination by narratives of historical events; what seizes upon Us so wonderfully is the disabuse of that innate faith in the fixity of the solid and sure- set foundations of the earth. From earlv child hood we are habituated to the contrast between the mobile element water, and the immobility of the soil on which we stand. All the evidences of our senses having confirmed this belief. But when suddenly the ground begins to rock beneath Us, the feeling of an unknown mysterious power in nature coming, and shaking the solid globe, arises in the mind. The illusion ot the whole of our earlier life is annihilated in an instant. We are undeceived as to the repose of nature, þÿ we feel ourselves transported to the realm, and made subject to the empire ol destructive unknown powers. I'.vciv sound þÿ the slightest rustle in the air þÿ sets attention on the slreicli- We uo longer host the earth

upon which we stand. The o usual in t he phenomenon throws ihe same anxious unrest and alarm over the lower animals. tSuiue and dogs are particularly affected by it ; and the verv crocodiles ot the Orinoco, otherwise as dumb as our little lizards, leave the shaken bed of the stream and lun bellowing into the Woods. To man, the earthquake presents itself as an all pervading unlimited something. We can temove fiom an active crater, from the stream of lava that is pouring down upon onr dwelling we can escape; with the earthquake we feel that whithersoever we fly, we are still on the earth of destruction. Such a mental condition, though Convoked in our very innermost nature, is not, however, ot long duiation. When a series of slighter shocks occur in another every trace of alarm soon vanishes among the inhabitants On the rainless coasts ol Feru, nothing is known of hail, not of explosions of lightning and rolling thunder in the bosom of the atmosphere. The subterraneous noise that accompanies the earthquake there comes in lieu of the thunder of the clouds. Use and wont for a series of years, and the very prevalent opinion that dangerous earthquakes are only to be apprehended two or three times in the course of a century, lead the inhabitants <d Lima scare !y to think more of a slight shock of anearihquake than is thought of a hail stone in lie temperate zone. þÿ Hnrnbtild's Survey vf Ihe Physical llislory of the heavens.

The New Orleans Courier of January 3rd with some information apparently not possessed by other papers of that city, discusses at large the probability of the success of Mr. þÿSlidell mission s to Mexico According to its views (as translated and condensed lor tbe Picayune) this success must depend upon the ability of the Government of Fresident Herrera to withstand the attack of Faredes. The Courier enters at length into the circumstances and position of both these chieftains, as well as of Generals Arista and Bustamente and thence it deduces the almost certain triumph of Faredes. But the principle upon which Faredes will go into power is that of unqualified resistance to the annexation of Texas to the United States, and to the dismemberment of the Mexican Republic. Hence, the Courier argues his suptemacy will be fatal to the hopes entertained of success for the American Minister. The latest account received at New Orleans brought a report that Faredes had declared against Herrera, and was marching upon the capital; but in tbe meantime the Government organ at Mexico has officially announced that Faredes had assured the Fresident that he would stand hv and support the Government in ncgociating with the United States, in case the popular clamor against making peace should endanger tiie safety of the Government.

A letter from Constantinople, of the 10th Dec. says þÿ þÿ The (estival of the Courban Bairam commenced yesterday morning. þÿ The Sultan, according to custom, slept the night before at the palace of Top Capon, and in the morning went in great pomp to the mosque of Sultan Ahmed, surrounded by all ollicers of state, in their grand ceremonial costumes. The suite ol the Sultan was ex tremely brilliant, and for some time past, whether from the troops being better dressed and disciplined, or from the preparations being made with greater attention to order, these public ceremonies have assumed a character ot grandeur and majesty which they did not formerly possess, and consequently they make a deeper impression upon tiie minds of the people. The þÿSultan d s ress was what it has been always since the reform. He wore a red cap, low in form, with a long tassel banging from it behind, and Surmounted in front by a diamond aigrette. A frock coat, with a straight collar, and buttoned in front from top to bottom, tight pantaloons with under straps, while gloves, and highlyvarnished leather boots. Ordinarily the Sultan wore a very full cloak or mantle, wrapped entirely around him ; but this day the cloak fastened to the deck with a rich diamond clasp, was suffered to float negligently over the shoulders, and thus exposed the whole of his person. The þÿSultan demean- s our was excellent. He rode a splendid and gallant horse, which he managed with great ease. He wore on his breast a profusion of

diamonds, and, by bis side, a seymilar, or curved sword, suspended from a girdle, which, as well as the sword, was loaded with precious stones. Thus accoutred, he rode with great majesty at the head of the procession A kiosk, standing near the gate of the palace through Which it was to come, had been prepared for the accommodation of the diplomatic corps and their families Baron and Baroness de Bmirqueney, Count and Countoss Stunner, the wile ot the first secretary of the British Embassy, Mrs. Wellesley, were assembled, and attended by I'uad Ellendi, chief dragoman of the Poile, who was commissioned to do the honours of the day, which he did with the greatest attention and the best grace. When passing in front of the kiosk the Sultan turned his face towards it with an expression which showed that he recognised those who were in it. þÿ1 heSultan- Mother having at her side Murad Eflendi, the eldest son of the Sultan, about five years old, and accompanied by several of the ladles of the imperial harem, attended the ceremony in a carriage drawn by four horses richly caparisoned. From the mosque the Sultan returned to the palace of Top Capon, where he received all the high functionaries, who came to congratulate him on the occasion. This year: to the general satisfaction, the visits which were formerly repeated between the great ollicers of state during the four days which the festival lasts were dispensed þÿwith.

Extraordinary Impulses þÿ 1 do not know a human being more incapable of letting an idea, a falsehood of imagination, run away with bis Mr. C 'sj sober judgment, lie has a habit, I shouldjsny more than most men, of tying himself down to matters of fact. 1 copy an extract from a diary ; it was taken down that night: þÿ "Mr. C has just told me the following very curious circumstance: Some years ago Mrs. C being not in good health, they determined to spend some weeks in the country. "WE'RE ALL COWARDS IN THE þÿDARK.' General Excelmans, one of þÿNapoleon s paladins, was at a dinner party, composed of some o! the survivors of the battle ot Waterloo, a few of their younger relatives, and the scion ot an ex king, on a visit from his home in America Some questions arose \ about bravery, when t he younger members of the company were electrified to hear the venerable and heroic Excelmans gravely and seriously declare, that men were all cowards in the dark ! The general smiled at their expressions of dissent, remarked that it was þÿ very like þÿyouth, and proceeded to tell the following anecdote in support of his strange declaration. þÿ There was a young hothead in the þÿEmperor s service, who horning for action, and his duty for a time affording no opportunity, at last resolved to fight a duel, and, accordingly, choosing to construe some remark or other of an older and superior officer into an insult, challenged hint. The ohier soldier, waving all considerations of rank, agreed to meet the young man. but on the following unusual terms The time snould be night, the place a room, þÿ in opposite corners of which they were to stand. þÿ The seconds having placed their men, were to withdraw outside the door, taking the candles with them. The word should he given without, when he who had the first tire should discharge his weapon, and the seconds hearing the lights should immediately rush in. þÿ These strange conditions were accepted, the time ariived, and the seconds placed the par-

ties as agreed upon ; withdrawing immediately, and leaving their men in the dark. Tiie word Was given, the tire was heard, the door was re opened, and there stood the elder of the two bolt upright in the corner, his adver- 3ary's ball having entered the wall so close to his head that the escape seemed little less than miraculous! It was now the old s> -Id þÿei s turn to tiie. They were again left in the dark, the Word was given from the outside, and instantaneously with the discharge, the seconds rushed in and found the challenger prostrate upon the floor, not having yet recovered himself from his trick to avoid the bait, which, on examination, it was found must have killed him. The young man was covered with confusion, and the seconds were overwhelming him with the expression of their scorn, when the veteran stopped them. þÿ Not so fast, my young triends," said he þÿ you will grow wiser. Where do you suppose 1 was at the first fire! On my hands and knees in the corner, but ma foi I I was up quicker than he 1 Portliest, Messieurs ve are all cowards in the dark!" þÿ This was an actual tact, and the elder ot the parties was uo other than Excel mans lunisell.

Mexico and Europe. þÿ Our readers will remember that several weeks since we gave the substance of a leading article in the London limes, in which it was very ably argued that the best possible results of the present state of things in Mexico tor the interests of European Powers, would be the re conquest laj Spain of hei former provinces. ll was conceded that Spain was too weak to attempt such an entetprise of herself: þÿ tint it was urged that it would he for the interests of England to extend her aid We remaiked at the time that in this fotm, through the Times, were often foreshadowed the actual purposes of the British Government. 1 his article, and these remarks, derive new interest fiont the statements contained in tltn þÿ following letter, published in the United Slates Gazette : þÿ Havana, January 3. 1840. Dear Sir: þÿ ! have heard numerous rumours that are floating about in this city, and will give you a few of them. There is no doubt of some grand scheme going foiward among the European Courts. One of the rumours is. that one of the sons of the King of prance is to marry the Infanta of Spain, and take possession of Mexico and give it back to Spain. The Court of Madrid will appoint the son of Louis Phiiiippe Regent of Mexico. There appears some truth in this rumor, as we have a large Spanish fleet in the harbor, and a large French fleet is expected here to act in concert with the Spanish. England will have a large number of ships of war to cruise in the Gulf ot Mexico.

What share of the sport England is to receive for Iter share, Madame Rumor does not say, but only hints at Upper California, or the Eastern half of Cuba, say to the longitude of 78, ns this part of the island will he nearer her possessions. I he Court of Madrid does not like the idea of giving England a foothold in Cuba as from this island Spain derives nearly all her revenue, and she knows full well that if England once raises the cross ot St. George iu Cuba, the w hole island is lost

to tier, and in lieu of this will offer to Vicious Porto Rico. Santa Ana is here, and :s a deep politician; fie is no doubt Irving to effect a revolution in Mexico through the army, by working on their feelings against the United States for annexing Texas. As Santa Ana is in the power o! the Spanish Government, lie wishes to make it appear that he is in favor of giving up Mexico to Spain; fie is in correspondence with all the Generals of Mexico, t s he receives several large packages by every steam packet from Vera Cruz. Santa Ana you will find to lead the European diplomatists on the wrong scent ; his object will fie to throw Mexico into the arms of the United States, just at the time the European Powers have all things arranged ; this he no doubt thinks will cause a war between France and Spain, in which England must take part with Spain. You will see that Spain, in her stupidity, will lose the Island of Cuba, as the Cubanians only want a pretext to declare themselves independent and have the Republic of Cuba. When tired of opprobriums and humiliations, you boldly shook off the ominous yoke, which a most cruel and tyrannical governnient had imposed upon you, you made known to the world your motives for separating from the Havtien people ; neither the had treatment you had experienced, nor the resentment you felt, caused you to depart from the paths of moderation and generosity which characterise you. lfon the on. hand you swore before God and man to spend ev'ry drop of your blood in defence of your religion your liberty, and your rights ; on the other you interposed and implored the mercy of the Omnipotent Being, that your adversaries might be disposed to a just and rational consideration, to avoid the effusion of blood and the calamities of a frightful war which we did not provoke, but which if it came to the point would be one of extermination, they being responsible for all the evils, which might arise through the unjust tenacity and obstinacy with which they deny our reasonable pretensions True to your promise ; your generous conduct is to be admired ; more than four thousand souls, adherents to the Havtien cause, have left your soil 5 their persons and property have been respected ; the promises given on capitulations have been faithfully kept þÿ the prisoners whom the fortune of war has thrown into our hands, have been treated according to the customs estah lished among civilized nations; and in accordance with the principles of the rights of

man þÿ we have kept within the limits of a defensive war, without trespassing beyond the ancient boundaries of our territory: proposals have been made to the representatives of the Havtien Government offering them arrangements in conformity with the rights of the respective people. They must be convinced that we cannot act contrary to the fundamental rights of the liberty <>f man and ot equality, which are the constitutives of our government ; yet every thing has been done in vain to induce them to show the same sentiment of justice and reason with which we have acted, and are disposed to defend a Holy cause, which has deserved grace before the creator, whose strong hand has opposed the enemies whenever tfiev have attempted to subdoe you, and again impose those humiliating and shameful chains which you dragged along during twenty two years captivity. Furiously ! and impiously ! they expanded terrible forces against our territories, leaving tracks of cruelty ami inhumanity wherever they trod ; your churchmen and warriors, who were disposed to defend those rights with Which nature has endowed man, were imprisoned ; manacled, thrown into filthy dungeons, famishing þÿ your brethren who were unfortunately unadvised of what was taking place, and were residing among them, were put in the van of their armies to he the first victims sacrificed. Far from granting you justice, far from hearing your complaints, the leaders of the Havtien have done nothing but crimson the war, saci dicing their prison-
ers and threatening us continually with total destruction. Government has just learned by late papers and advices received front Puerto

0 'll D 1 AT as Principe, that the Hayliens are preparing a large force to match against the eastern part and that their plans are to lay waste the country and to give no quarter, either to men, women, or children. 1 am well aware that if their intentions were such they would not make them known, but zealous for your glory and the preservation of the countiy, whatever be 1 he difficulties which may frustrate their plans, my duty is to warn you of the danger which threatens y ou. From Hell's Weekly Messenger, London January 20, 1840, THE þÿQUEEN S SPEECH.

HOUSE OF LORDS. þÿ Thursday, Jan. 22. Her .Majesty, accompanied by the Prince Consort, went in state this day to the House of Peers to open the session of parliament. þÿ Her Majesty, who looked in good health, having taken her seat on the Throne (Prince Albert occupying the chair of state on her left), and having desired the peers and others, who had risen at her entrance, to be seated, Black Rod was directed to command the immediate attendance of the House of Commons at the bar. This summons, after the lapse of a few minutes, having been obeyed þÿ a large number of the lower house crowding below the bar þÿ her Majesty delivered the following gracious Speech ; þÿ þÿ Lords and Gentlemen , Uy þÿ It gives me great satisfaction again to meet you in parliament, and to have the opportunity of recurring to your assistance and advice. þÿ I continue to receive from mV allies and from all other foreign powers the stiongest assurances of their desire to cultivate the most friendly relations with this country. þÿ I rejoice that in concert with the Emperor of Russia, and through the success of our joint mediation, I have been enabled to adjust the differences which had long prevailed between the Ottoman Porte and the King of Prussia, and had seriously endangered the tranquillity of the East. þÿ For several years a desolating and sanguinary warfare has afflicted the states of the Rio de la Plata. The commerce of all nations has been interrupted, and acts of barbarity have been committed unknown to the

practice of civilised people. In conjunction with the King of the French. I am endeavouring to effect the pacification of those states. þÿ The convention concluded with France in the course of the last year, for the more effectual suppression of the slave trade, is about to be carried into immediate execution, by the active co operation of the two powers on the coast of Africa. þÿ It is my desire that our present union and the good understanding Iwliich so happily exists between us may always be employed to promote the interests of humanity, and to secure the peace of the world. " I regret that the conflicting claims of Great Britain and the United States, in respect of the territory on the north western coast of America, although they have been made the subject of repeated negociation, still remain unsettled. þÿ You may be assured that no effort, consistent with national honour, shall bo wanting on my part to bring this question to an early and peaceful termination. þÿ Gentlemen of the House of Commons, þÿ The estimates for the year will be laid before vou at an early period. þÿ Although I am deeply sensible of the importance of enforcing economv in all branches of the expenditure, yet I have been compelled, hv a due regard to the exigencies of the public service, and to the state of our naval and military establishments, to propose some increase in the estimates which provide for their efficiency.

S Vt% ® 3$ '612 A T 2 3. - ..i þÿ Lords and Gentlemen, My þÿ 1 have observed with deep regret, the Very frequent instances in which the crime of deliberate assassination has been of late com mined in Ireland. It will he your duty to consider whether any measures can he devised calculated to give increased protection to life, and to bring to justice the perpetratois of so dreadful a crime. þÿ I have to lament that in consequence of a failure of the potato crop in several parts of the United Kingdom, there w ill he a deficient supply of an article of food which forms the chief subsistence of great numbers of my people. The disease by which the plant lias been affected has prevailed to the greatest extent in Ireiand. þÿ 1 have adopted all such precautions as it was in my power to adopt, for the purpose of alleviating the sullerings which may he caused by this calamity, and I shall confidently rely on Votti co-operation in devising such other means for effecting the same benevolent purpose as may requite the sanction of the legislature. þÿ I have had great satisfaction in giving my assent to the measures which you have presented to me from time to time calculated to extend commerce, and to stimulate domestic. skill and industry, by the repeal of prohibitory and the relaxation oi protective duties. þÿ The prosperous slate of the revenue, the increased demand for labour, and the general improvement which Iras taken place in the internal condition of the country, arc strong

testimonies in favour of the course yon have pursued. I recommend you to take into vour early consideration whether the principles on which you have acted may not with advantage he yet more extensively applied, and whether it may not be in your power, after a careful review of the existing duties upon many articles the produce or manufacture of other countries, to make such further reduction and remission as may tend to insure the continuance of the great benefits to which 1 have adverted, and, by enlarging our commercial intercourse, to strengthen the bonds of amity witli foreign powers. þÿ Any measures which you may adopt for effecting these great objects will, I am convinced, be accompanied hy such precautions as shall prenent permanent loss to the revenue or injurious results to any of the great interests of the country, þÿ I have full reliance on your just and dispassionate considcratiou of matters so deeply affecting the public welfare. þÿ It is my earnest prayer that, with the blessings of Divine Providence on your councils, you may be enabled to promote friendly feelings between different classes of my subjects, provide additional security for the continuance of peace, and to maintain content nient and happiness at home by increasing the comforts and bettering the condition of the great body of iny people." Her Majesty having concluded her address, rose from the throne, and quitted the house with the same state as she entered. The numerous assemblage then separated, and
their lordships adjourned during pleasure. -store- American Maii.s, and the Question of Peace or War þÿ The letters and papers which have been delivered by these

þÿI I . I T mails are rendered more than usually impor tant bv the peculiar circumstances of the limes; we must add however, that much of their importance is ill appearance only, and results rather from the excited apprehension of the monied men in the City, titan from any well founded judgment upon the intrinsic character of the case itself. Taken partially the proceedings in the Senate seem to threaten war, but upon, a more quiet and leisurely examination, we cun unhesitatingly sav that we fear no result of tins kind. In the Ameti can Chambers, as in otfier popular assemblies there are some imprudent hot headed men, intemperate and pugnacious in themselves, and further employing this tone of speaking in order to recommend them -elves to the vanity and self glory of t heir own countrymen. But tins is not the character of the Senate itself, and it is gratifying to see that Mr. Calhoun, Mr. Miles. Mr. Crittiden, Mr Webster, and Mr. Clayton, all of them leaders in the American Senate, and men of more temper and gravity, are all contending in a contrary direction, and that all of them express the same opinions þÿ that under present eiicumsiances they anticipate no adverse and extreme conclusion to the pending negociation, and can see neither necessity nor reasonable grounds tor the apprehension of a war between England and the United States. The most important debate, the one immediately beating upon peace or war, is reported at length in these papers; it occurred in

the Senate on the last night but one of the past year, and was opened hy a set of resolutions proposed by Mr. Harmegan, one of the leaders of the war party. The resolutions were in substance, that ali the country within the parallels of 42 and 54 north latitude known as the Oregon district, is t he property and part and parcel of the territory of the United States: that the President had no power to transfer its soil and the allegiance of its citizens to any foreign power ; and therefore that the President had exceeded his constitutional prerogative in proposing it as the basis of the pending negociation. To this set of resolutions Mr. Calhoun immediately proposed a series of counter resolutions ; declaring in substance þÿ that the President has the power, with the advice of the Senate, to make treaties, and that the settlement of boundary lines is embraced in this power; that in offering in a spoil of peace and harmony the 49(li parallel ns the dividing line between the United States and Great Britain, the President exercised powers rightfully belonging to him, and acted for the best interests of the þÿcountry Though the debate upon these resolutions was deferred to the middle of the current month, enough occurred in the Senate to indicate that the feeling of the house was with Mr. Calhoun. Mr. Miles, a verv influential senator, and a supporter of the government, almost repealed Mr. þÿCalhoun s words, that the President was of the same feeling and opinion with Mr. Calhoun, and

would concur with him in the maintenance ol peace It was true, lie said that the negociation had been broken off, yet it could and probably would be resumed. þÿ Whether it was wise in our government to have renewed the oiler made on former occasions, bv wav of compromise to divide the territory upon the 49th degree of north latitude, he would not pronounce an opinion, but having made

that offer, and withdrawn it after it had been declined, he could not see how it well could he refused, should Great Britain hereafter propose that as the basis for compromising the þÿdispute. The comments of the New York Courier upon this debate are worthy of much attention both for their due gravity and sound good sense. þÿ Our own conclusion is," says the intelligent editor, þÿ that the decision of the question of war or peace is in the hands of the British government. Can they, lor the mere barren triangle of land which constitutes the dillerence between what they ask and we have offered, be willing to put at hazard the peace of the world ? For a war between the United Stales and England would not long he confined to those two powers þÿ We entirely concur in these remarks, and wi'h their obvious result, that in the manifest tone of the American Senate, in the courteous and ordinary proceedings of the American negociators, and in the actual friendly tone of the two governments. there is an end of all reasonable apprehension of war; to say nothing of the most insignificant value of the object concerned. A war, indeed, from the very commencement of the discussion, could upon our part onlv have two objects ; first, a vindication ot our national honour on the point of t lie arrogant and defying language employed by the President in his first claim ; and secondly the acquisition ot the barren desert to the Oregon. As to the first of these objects, it is already obtained ; the President and the

government have already made sufficient amends for their former incivility bv their present respect and uniform courtesy : lor as to the violent language ot one or mote individual members of the Chambers, we might as reasonably impute it to the government, as we could reasonably make the master of a house responsible for the dogs which were harking at him from without. As to the value of the Oregon, and its adequacy to constitute a cause of war in itself, there cannot exist two opinions upon the subject. It is utterly worthless to us, and must remain so for three hundred years to come. þÿ Ibid Jan. 1!).

The present position of the country, in respect to its foreign relations, naturally directs the minds of men towards the best methods of putting the country in a defensive situation should any dilficulty grow out of our relations towards any foreign nation. Within the last few years, we have heard much of various improvements in every thing connected with art, in naval and military atiairs. The next war belween any two powerful nations, will be quite different from any thing which has heretofore been seen in the world. Since the termination of the last war, steam has been introduced into naval operations, and this alone would produce a perfect revolution in military and naval tactics. There are however certain statements made relating to a invention lately discovered m this neighbourhood, which we have no doubt will astonish the world, and will satisfy every one that we are on the eve ot a gieater

3 !P 'Ji <D 1 X at a a. revolution, in military and naval atiairs. than even the most sanguine mind could possibly imagine. During the last few months a series of experiments have been made with a new invention, originated by Mr. þÿMc Carthy, a gentleman connected with the Navy Yard at Brooklyn. These experiments were oidered bv the Government, a i.d witnessed by distinguished persons, and were considered by them as the most novel, most original, and most startling in a military point of view. Commander Stewart, it will be remembered spoke of a project by which it would be possible to defend ihe harbor of New York agaim the combined fleets ot all the powers of ibe world. This may appear to be gasconade, but from information which has been communicated to us, we are fully assuied that Commodore þÿStewart sassertion is perfectly correct and literal. The scientific gentleman alluded to, Mr. þÿMc þÿ t ariliv, who is now connected with the Navy Yard, lias invented a new species of ai idler v, which will discharge thirty halls in a minute, or one every two seconds lor hours in succession, and ibis from mechanical power alone, without gunpowder, chemical substance or any other preparation. It is effected bv pulling ihe bans into a hopper and allowing the oidnance to throw them out wiih nu immense momentum, at the rate ol one everv two seconds. On one occasion, Mr. Mc'Ciirthv exhibited the operation ol this invention in the Navy Yard, before a number of r.aval officers who were all astonished

bv the force and power exhibited, as well as bv t lie great simplicity ot I he machine. The principle of this new invention is simplv a modification of the punciple of the sling, applied to machinery, in connection with a tube or gun, throwing out u discharge of balls. The machine is so constructed that on putting in at one end the balls to tie discharged, a rotatory motion is produced by means of a crank, and, by a lew rapid revolutions, each ball receives a momentum equal to dial of gunpowder. When tins has been done, a slide starts and allows each hall to escape in succession from the chamber into a lube, when they are thrown to almost any distance and with an unerring aim. This ingenious invention for which a patent lias been taken out at Washington, and which ought to be purchased, is worth five hundred þÿ nay, even millions, to the American Government, in the present, crisis of its atiairs. By means of such machines placed in the Narrows, capable of discharging any number of balls of any calibre, the whole combined fleets of Europe could be torn in pieces and annihilated before they reached the battery at New York.

Fifteen sleutn bouts make a mile; this is anew rule of arithmetic, only found out in America, and, 1 mention it because it is much more easy than to remember that they are 850 feet long each. The Americans of all classes are travelling people, eminently so as confined to their own conn try ; but they know nothing of any other countries The United States is large enough, they think, to satisfy the most greedy o! travellers ; and tiie price of travelling is so cheap that, as the whole population live in boarding houses, it is as cheap to be travelling as to be stopping home, at if yon can apply such a word as home to a boardinghouse. For instance, in these moving palaces, which go twice a day to Albany, J50 miles, as far as Margate and hack again, 1 paid 2 s , hut I might have gone the same day for Is , by an other boat not quite so new and splendid.
